Considering that three years ago, insurance companies agreed to create a monopoly to establish the assessment basis and premium rates; that since that time, the rates as well as the assessment increased threefold, at least in Quebec; that the assessment is based on the replacement value; and finally that for all those reasons, 70 per cent of small property owners and businessmen cannot afford insurance, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):

an intolerable rate, affecting low income families in particular, and since many producers have not received an increase in their prices for almost two years, how does the minister explain the unacceptable increases in food prices at the present time? subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-GOVERNMENT PLANS TO MEET SITUATION

speechtext: The general objective of that policy is to provide a transportation system that effectively supports the achievement of national and -regional, economic and social objectives, is efficient and ensures a high degree of accessibility and equity for all users.

speechtext:
We also emphasized throughout the new policy that there should be an efficient integration of the various modes of transportation by each service so that the best level of service is provided at the lowest possible cost.
The new policy recognizes, contrary to some elements of the 1967 National Transportation Act, that transportation in Canada is a mix of services, varying in the degree of development and maturity and in the degree of competition.
Our view is that the role of the government should vary according to the nature of the services and region concerned. Those services which are well developed and mature should be operated on a commercially viable basis within a general policy and regulatory framework provided by the government. Hence, in those cases where there is effective competition, rates and services should be determined largely through the forces of the marketplace. Yet in other regions or in other parts of the transportation system where services are required in the national or regional interest, but cannot achieve commercial viability or the required degree of technological development, the federal government is prepared to provide active support and financial assistance.
March 1, 1977

It has sometimes been suggested that our policy involves competition between the two concepts of commercial viability on the one hand and, on the other, the use of transportation as an instrument for the achievement of economic and social goals. The government does not see these concepts as conflicting but, rather, as complementary and mutually reinforcing. Because there appears to be some public misunderstanding on the point-a misunderstanding on the part of my noisy friends opposite-I should like to take a little time to explain how we see the relationship between those two objectives. The starting point is the proposition that it is the responsibility of government to see to it that the national transportation system-

speechtext: -provides freight and passenger services which adequately and efficiently meet the economic and social needs of Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
This is true whether or not the users of each individual service can reasonably afford to pay the full costs of providing that service. There are, and probably will always be, some services which are required in order to meet legitimate economic and social needs such as regional development or access to remote communities but for which the particular users cannot reasonably be expected to pay the full costs. In such cases government support in the form of direct or indirect subsidy is necessary and reasonable. Government support of this kind to ensure the provision of necessary transportation facilities which cannot be commercially viable represents the use of transportation as an instrument for the achievement of economic and social objectives. But the resources available to government for these purposes are necessarily limited and should always be used for maximum effect because the legitimate claims upon them are extensive. It is therefore important, Mr. Speaker, that available resources be conserved for application to those situations where they are most needed, and not dissipated in support of transportation services which may only be convenient but not necessary or of other services which are necessary but capable of commercial viability without subsidy.
Subsidies so often distort the picture and hide real costs, so that more is spent in total on transportation than would have been without the distortion. That is waste; this is not cost effective. Wherever we can, therefore, we shall make decisions based on real costs. Where even the lowest cost is too high for someone to pay we should help him, if we see his needs, to have the service. Most often we should help him but leave him free to find the lowest cost and most effective transportation.
Given that policy approach, my purpose today, on behalf of the Minister of Transport is twofold: first, to give what is more or less a progress report to the House on several of the major
National Transportation Act
initiatives which the government has undertaken or is about to undertake to implement that new transportation policy and, second, to introduce proposed amendments to the National Transportation Act, the Railway Act, the Transport Act and the Department of Transport Act in order to implement the new policy in areas that require changes to existing legislation. For the first purpose it might be useful to outline our activities in freight and then in passenger transportation.
Over the past few years we have undertaken a number of initiatives, often with the provinces, carriers and industries concerned, to move freight more effectively and efficiently within, to and from Canada. Some of our efforts have a regional orientation, others are more national in scope. In western Canada, various developments are under way or are in an advanced stage of planning. First, we are involved in a number of activities to improve and increase the capacity of the rail system to move commodities within the region and to export markets. These include the improvement of the CN and CP main lines through the Rockies and the prairies, the development of the northern British Columbia rail system and an examination of the possibilities of joint track usage.
Second, we are taking various steps to change and modernize the grain handling system, including the purchase of hopper cars, investments in new or improved terminal facilities, and recommendations of the Hall and Snavely commissions. Third, we have or will be adopting measures to add to the capacity, efficiency and annual throughput of port facilities in centres such as Prince Rupert and Vancouver. Finally, we are making investments in the primary highway networks of the prairies and in the development of highways in the western northlands.
In central and eastern Canada a similar range of freight transportation efforts is under way or planned, including port expansions and improvements at such centres as Quebec City, Saint John and Halifax; capital investments and essential research and development to increase the utilization of the St. Lawrence Seaway and the Great Lakes through lock and channel improvements and through the development of marine shunters and air-cushion icebreaking vehicles; and measures to increase efficiency and capacity in the railway system and in ferry freight operations and the highway network, particularly in the Atlantic region.
Northern Canada has historically also had unique transportation problems and needs. We are dealing with these through increased funding for air transportation infrastructure, continuing support for the Northern Transportation Company Ltd., improved Arctic resupply services, joint industry-government investment in the MV Arctic bulk carrier, and the analysis of future marine investments for the north, including perhaps a larger polar icebreaker to assist in the exploration and development of Arctic natural resources. Each of these efforts is aimed at meeting the development needs and potential of each region of the country by ensuring that the basic freight transportation system is there to accommodate and, where necessary, to stimulate industrial and commercial growth.

March 1, 1977
National Transportation Act
Besides these regional thrusts, freight transportation initiatives more national in scope are under way or planned. Soon the government hopes to table in this House legislation to establish largely autonomous port commissions at 20 ports of national significance and to improve the co-ordination and direction of all transportation port activity through the creation of a Canadian ports commission within the Department of Transport.
The methods of regulating freight transportation as well as passenger transportation are in continuous need of change and improvement as freight movements grow in quantity, variety and complexity and as traffic flows shift from one mode to another or from one trade area to another. The CTC has made a number of determined attempts to improve the efficiency of its regulatory process, especially in the area of rail transportation. The new legislative proposals which will be outlined shortly should help in freeing scarce resources in the CTC, enabling it to focus more exclusively on its regulatory functions. The proposed changes should also provide a more effective legal basis for rail freight regulations. While for a variety of reasons the federal role in truck regulation has never been clear since 1967, the government is hopeful that as a result of current discussions with the provinces and industry we will be able to fashion a more effective federal-provincial partnership in that important regulatory area.
A final freight transportation matter of broader national implication is the systematic analysis of various direct and indirect freight subsidies and assistance programs. These range from branch line subsidies through grain freight rate assistance and St. Lawrence Seaway deficits to Atlantic region freight rate subsidies. Most of these were implemented when the economic and transportation needs of the west, Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces were significantly different from what they will be in the coming decade. Some of these programs, however well-intentioned and effective years ago, now actually inhibit the development of certain regions and of parts of the transportation system. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport has proposed changes in a number of these assistance programs. We think that these changes will lead to a more efficient, effective and productive transportation system.
Another important element of the new transportation policy is the recognition that passenger problems are every bit as real to the country as freight transportation problems and that the challenge of moving people in the most effective and efficient manner increasingly calls for a multimodal approach; that is, an approach which emphasizes that every mode, whether it is air, rail, bus or car should be encouraged where it is likely to be the most effective. In the context of that approach the Minister of Transport announced last January a policy on rail passenger services. In the light of unacceptably high financial losses and deteriorating services in recent years on rail passenger operations, the government's objectives are to revitalize those services which are essential and potentially effective and encourage other modes to replace rail services which are no longer justified.

The Canadian Transport Commission recently issued a summary report on transcontinental rail passenger services following extensive public hearings on this subject. It is currently giving priority, as directed in the rail passenger policy statement, to the development of a plan for transcontinental and regional rail services in western and central Canada. As service is improved and subsidy per passenger decreased, it is the government's intent to increase its subsidy from 80 per cent to 100 per cent of losses. We are also negotiating with CN and CP for the establishment of a Canadian rail passenger corporation that will operate, manage and market the improved service across the country, Via Canada.
To demonstrate the possibilities of improved rail passenger services the government has chosen the Quebec-Windsor corridor. The first phase of the corridor improvement project, affecting the Quebec City-Montreal segment, has already begun. Over the next three years the government will spend approximately $30 million on this segment in order to acquire modern, high-speed trains and to improve rail lines, signals and maintenance facilities. Let me stress that it is also our aim to make improvements in several rail services in other areas of the country. Following completion of the CTC hearings, the remaining transcontinental and regional rail passenger services in every part of the country, not just in the Quebec-Windsor corridor, will be improved.
The broader multimodal approach to transportation has also caused the federal government to focus more closely on interprovincial bus transportation, the role of the automobile and the future need for urban transportation. We are working with the provinces to consider ways and means of improving bus transportation in certain parts of the country; the Atlantic region is one example. While there may never be enough financial resources to meet all needs for urban transportation, we believe that we have launched a number of positive steps, through the rail relocation, grade crossing and commuter rail programs, to improve public transportation in urban areas.
It has been the view of a number of Canadians, and perhaps even some members of this House, that in its approach to passenger transportation the federal Department of Transport has historically been unduly oriented toward the air mode at the expense of bus and rail. Certainly, the rail passenger initiatives I just mentioned should alleviate that concern. But it should also be kept in mind that the demand for air transportation has grown in leaps and bounds over the past two decades and, despite some cyclical slowdowns, is likely to continue to increase substantially in the future.
Hence, new facilities and services have been and will continue to be provided wherever necessary and desirable. Yet at the same time I would like to inform members that additional measures have been implemented recently to ensure that airports and air services are developed and approved, where the case is sound, with standards and facilities which the air industry and Canadians both need and can afford. In some way, our air services and facilities have been so good that we
March 1, 1977

have perhaps come to expect too much; we may have to lower our level of expectations unless we are prepared to pay more through increased government expenditures and, hence, increased taxes.
While on the subject of government expenditures and taxes for transportation purposes, I might once again tell hon. members briefly why this government is so concerned about the need to increase the level of cost recovery from transportation services. As we all know, most Canadians are worried about rising government expenditures and about growing government involvement in almost every aspect of Canadian society. There is a general desire-sometimes I wonder whether it is shared by members opposite-to limit government spending and government involvement, and that desire applies to certain aspects of transportation as well. Where possible, the growth in government expenditures should be reduced and activities left to the individual, to the local community or to private enterprise.
Federal transportation expenditures have increased rapidly. For example, over the past five years the combined budget of the Department of Transport, including Transport Canada Financing of Crown corporations, and the Canadian Transport Commission has almost doubled from $834.5 million in 197071 to $1,646.6 million in 1975-76. In this latter year our deficit for the provision of air services across the country totalled $448 million; ferry subsidies, largely in the Atlantic provinces, accounted for another $110.5 million; freight subsidies, east and west, were $118 million; rail passenger subsidies, $160 million; while the current debt of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority and its 1975-76 operating and maintenance losses are $817 million and $17 million respectively. Besides accounting for more than one half of our total 1-975-76 budget, these deficits and subsidies are increasing at a very rapid rate. For example, it has been predicted that without the positive government initiative 1 referred to earlier, the 1980 subsidies for rail passenger services alone would be approximately $400 million as compared with the 1975-76 figure of $160 million.
These subsidies also often distort the choice by users and consumers of the most economically efficient transportation means and have in the past led to real or imagined regional discrimination. For example, while in 1972 governments at all levels subsidized rail and air passengers by five cents and two cents per mile respectively, the bus passenger received no subsidy at all. Surely we should not bias the passenger's choice among competing travel modes in this way. This is particularly true in cases where the bias is counter to other important objectives such as environmental quality or energy efficiency.
In freight transportation a number of bulk commodity movements are currently subsidized through such mechanisms as the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority and the Crowsnest pass rates agreement. Finally, certain regions of the country often voice objections, many of them valid, that the direct or indirect subsidization of freight and passenger movements in one region inhibits the necessary development of industries and communities in other regions. Hence, our transportation deficits and subsidies are not only large and increasing rapidly;
National Transportation Act
they are also often unfair and discriminatory. In addition, subsidies frequently tend to encourage inefficiency; the more one subsidizes a service, the fewer are the incentives to remain or to become efficient.
In light of these facts I think all members will agree that the federal government must ask whether the present variety of expensive subsidy programs and deficits is providing Canadians with the best possible return per dollar spent on transportation and whether they should be allowed to increase at such a rapid rate. Unless we can control our transportation expenditures, and unless we insist that whenever possible the users of these transportation services pay a greater proportion of the actual cost themselves, the taxpayer will simply have to pay more taxes or the government will have to increase its deficits. And as my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), has pointed out repeatedly, that is simply not realistic in times of economic difficulty and in light of the general desire of most Canadians for fiscal restraint by all levels of government.
It is within this context that the agreement proposed, and discussed with many formally and informally, a policy of cost effectiveness; that is, to see how our deficits and subsidies can be reoriented to make them more effective, more equitable and as inexpensive to the taxpayer as possible. The policy basically implies that whenever national or regional, economic or social ends do not justify a transportation subsidy, then the user of the facility or service should pay. This certainly does not mean that all transportation services should be fully paid for by their users, regardless of circumstances. If that were the case, many necessary services such as air connections to remote northern communities or maritime ferry services, to mention a few obvious examples, would simply disappear.
That certainly is not our objective. If only for this reason, we have no doubt that government subsidies will continue to play a significant role in our national transportation system. Yet surely it makes sense that users should pay the cost of transportation services where it is economically practical for them to do so. Then the limited funds available for subsidies can be reserved for those special situations where necessary transportation services cannot earn sufficient revenues to cover their costs and can only be provided with government assistance.
These subsidy funds can and will be used to stimulate slow-growth regions and to provide essential transportation services. In the Atlantic provinces, the minister has discussed with the provincial premiers different alternatives for reallocating transportation funds to assist regional air, bus, rail and highway improvements. In the west, the federal government has helped in the strengthening of prairie highways and is implementing programs to encourage prairie air services and the movement of rapeseed products. I am somewhat startled at the ruckus we have seen in the last few days against my colleague, the Minister of Transport, sitting down with the mayor of Saskatoon and working out a general agreement for the improvement of the airport and the development of plans

speechtext:
In British Columbia we are studying the future development of transportation infrastructure for the movement of regional resources, especially coal. In other words, by changing existing subsidy programs that are not totally effective we can reallocate scarce funds for more essential development purposes.
Mr. Speaker, I think the initiatives I have mentioned so far demonstrate the government's intention to adopt the positive yet selective role envisaged in our new transportation policy. But I want to stress that this role has not been exercised unilaterally. We have been, and intend to continue, planning and implementing changes in consultation and often in conjunction with the provinces, the carriers, industry, labour and the public at large. For example, over the past few years we have established formal federal-provincial committees for each of the western, Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic regions so that at both the ministerial and officials level there will be regular contact, dialogue and co-operation on major transportation issues. We have also improved our consultative mechanisms with the major carriers such as CN, CP, Air Canada, CP Air, with the regional air carriers and with carrier associations and industry groups too numerous to list in full today. Suffice it to say here that the list includes such carrier associations as the Dominion Marine Association, Canadian Trucking Association, port groups, the Air Transport Association of Canada and the Canadian Motor Coach Association, and such industry groups as the Canadian Industrial Traffic League and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this quick progress report has been of some assistance to the House in informing the members, if only in a general way, about the approach to and main elements of our transportation initiatives. It will, I hope, also help to set the stage for the second subject which I wish to address today: the main elements of the transport policy legislative proposals which the Miniser of Transport would like to introduce for second reading. There are three main elements of the legislation: first, proposed changes and additions to the transportation policy objectives and principles under section 3 of the National Transportation Act; second, proposed changes and additions to the National Transportation Act and the Department of Transport Act relating to the responsibilities of the Minister of Transport and the Canadian Transport Commission; third, proposed amendments to the Railway Act, the National Transportation Act, and the Transport Act, relating to the legislation governing the regulation of railway freight rates.
The proposed revised statement of objectives and principles under section 3 of the National Transportation Act reflects the new policy thrust outlined in June, 1975, by the former minister of transport in his statement to the House. The
(Mr. Basford.)
amendments now being introduced have been discussed with provincial governments, the carriers and other interested parties. The government's intent, in proposing the revised statement of objectives and principles, is to retain those elements of the National Transportation Act which continue to be relevant to present requirements. At the same time, the changes and additions in the proposed legislation are significant. Our main proposals consist of four basic points: first, a statement which establishes that it is the objective of the transportation policy for Canada to achieve a transportation system that is efficient, is an effective instrument of support for the achievement of national and regional social and economic objectives, and is accessible and equitable. The concept of efficiency in the present act is not lost, but more emphasis is placed on service to Canadians and on the support of national and regional objectives. When this is referred to committee, the minister will propose, once having completed consultation with the provinces, some amendments to the transportation policy objective which will further strengthen the government's commitment to link transportation with the achievement of national and regional objectives.
Second, the recognition of the need for co-operation between the different levels of government, as well as consultation with the public in major aspects of the development and economic regulation of the transportation system. It certainly is our intention that no major policy initiatives will be put forward unless there has been a full and frank process of consultation with the provinces concerned. While, of course, this has to be a two-way process, we are firmly of the belief that by doing so we will have more effective policies and a better transportation system.
Third, a principle establishing the explicit goal of over-all commercial viability for the transportation system, yet allowing for financial assistance by the government when necessary, especially when the achievement of national or regional objectives requires it. Here, too, my colleague will propose an amendment in committee to ensure that the achievement of national and regional objectives is an overriding objective relative to the objective of commercial viability.
Fourth, the recognition that where effective competition exists, transportation rates and services should be established by the market place, but where it does not exist, rates and services should be regulated so as to give users the same protection they would have if effective competition existed.
These principles have the most immediate relevance for domestic transportation, but they also have relevance for the international shipping on which Canada's well-being as a major trading nation is highly dependent. By reason both of technological change and the policies which other countries are adopting to meet their national aspirations-policies and aspirations with which we have no basic quarrel-the competitive nature of international shipping is changing. In light of that change, Canada's own international shipping policy, which is basically one of reliance on free competition to provide adequate and economic services for our shippers, may require adjustment. This whole area is under review and it is already
March 1, 1977

clear that we require legislation to enable us to work constructively with countries which prefer not to rely entirely on free competition to assure the carriage of our bilateral trade.
A second main element in the package of legislative proposals being introduced today involves proposed amendments to the section of the National Transportation Act which states the responsibilities of the Minister of Transport and of the Canadian Transport Commission. As early as 1973, the then minister of transport forcefully expressed his concern at the lack of authority which the minister has under the present legislation to ensure that adequate transportation policies are developed and implemented in the national interest. The amendments that are now being proposed can be viewed as part of the government's adoption of a more positive role in the provision of an effective national transportation system, which at the same time maintains the essential role of the CTC as a regulatory body.
Hence, the proposed changes and additions to the National Transportation Act include first, clarification that it is the responsibility of the Minister of Transport to undertake the necessary measures to achieve the objective of the transportation policy, consistent with the proposed revised statement of principles which 1 have just discussed. This involves the addition of the proposed section 3(3) of the act which specifies the responsibility of the minister. Second, the amendment of section 22 to transfer a number of policy advisory functions to the department. The commission would retain the regulatory powers it has relating to licensing, authorizing or requiring the operation of and controlling the rates and tariffs for those modes of transport under its jurisdiction.
Third, the addition of section 3.1(1) to permit the governor in council, by order, to transfer to the minister any powers, duties or functions conferred or imposed on the Canadian Transport Commission by this act or any other act; this section would not authorize the transfer of any power, duty or function relating to the commission's regulatory responsibilities for licensing, authorizing or requiring the operation of and controlling the rates and tariffs for any mode of transport.
Fourth, amendments to sections 3 and 22 which would permit the minister to transfer powers to the commission to be exercised on his behalf, and request the commission to undertake research and investigation that would be of assistance to him in the exercise of his powers.
Fifth, addition of section 3.2 to permit the governor in council, on the recommendation of the minister, to issue general policy directives to the Canadian Transport Commission; this section stipulates that each such directive shall be without specific reference to any particular matter before the commission.
The third main part of the government's transport policy legislation proposes certain amendments to the legislation governing the regulation of railway freight rates. Under the National Transportation Act of 1967 the Canadian railways have been generally free, with the important exception of the
National Transportation Act
statutory grain rates, to set railway freight rates without regulatory approval so long as the rates are filed with the Canadian Transport Commission. The existing legislation under the Railway Act does include a minimum rate provision to prevent the railways from providing services on an non-compensatory basis, and a maximum rate provision to give some means of relief to shippers who rely exclusively on rail. However, these provisions in the Railway Act have been largely inoperative, and the so-called "public interest" clause-section 23 of the National Transportation Act-has given rise to frequent complaints from shippers about the costly and protracted nature of the regulatory process.
The rate-making freedom of the railways has been of concern to a number of provinces and shippers. Many firms are still largely dependent on rail transportation and often on one particular railway. In the case of bulk commodities, market competition has often been successful in reducing rates, but this success has been much less apparent in the movement of the more highly manufactured goods, especially those from central Canada to western markets. Our proposals to amend the legislation governing railway freight rates are generally intended to promote a greater degree of fairness, both regionally and to shippers, while taking into account the financial need of the Canadian railways. The government envisages that Canadian railways should continue to exercise considerable freedom in establishing freight rates where competitive forces can be expected to protect the public interest. Nevertheless, because of the importance of the railway system to the national economy, and the continued existence of some railway monopoly power in certain markets, it is proposed that the maximum and minimum rate provisions of the Railway Act should be strengthened.
The government acknowledges that maximum-minimum rules for regulating railway freight rates cannot be effective without a measure of railway costs which is accurate and which can be efficiently administered. Consequently, we intend to defer proclamation of the proposed amendments governing the establishment of new maximum and minimum rate rules until the Canadian Transport Commission has reviewed the 1969 railway costing order and has revised it through the public hearing process under section 330 of the Railway Act. We believe that the costing order requires revision in light of the economic and technological changes which have occurred since 1969.
Once a better costing system is developed, the government proposes that the present rules under the Railway Act should be amended. The principal amendments would be as follows: first, implementation of a more effective maximum rate provision which would grant discretionary powers to the governor-in-council to vary or eliminate the present "key weight"-of 30,000 pounds per carload-and to reduce the maximum add-on from the present 150 per cent above variable cost down to 100 per cent above variable cost. It is also proposed to make the maximum rate provision available to all shippers, instead of the present limitation to "captive" shippers.

Second, other legislative changes to ensure adequate enforcement of both the minimum and the maximum rate provisions. It is proposed to establish penalty clauses for the violation of these provisions, with the railways being liable for financial payments in the case of such violations. In the case of the minimum rate provision, this would continue to be based on variable cost, as redefined under the proposed new costing order, with an additional provision under the Railway Act which, if implemented, would require the CTC to annually submit to the Minister of Transport a report on any investigations of railway freight rates which are possibly below variable costs.
In addition to changing the maximum-minimum provisions of the Railway Act the government proposes to amend section 23 of the National Transportation Act in order to establish time limits for the handling of freight rate cases under this section by the CTC at the prima facie stage, while maintaining the discretionary authority of the regulatory body where leave to appeal has been granted. This proposal is intended to expedite the hitherto protracted nature of investigations under this section, while at the same time maintaining due process. The CTC will also continue its general efforts to improve administrative procedures in freight rate cases.
Finally, it is proposed to introduce an amendment which would directly address, for the first time, the problem of long-haul/short-haul rate differentials. The proposed amendment would require the CTC, on the basis of a complaint, to prohibit such rate differentials except where the CTC is satisfied that owing to competition it is expedient to allow such a differential to exist. This proposal is intended to modify an element of railway pricing which has been perceived, especially in the prairie provinces, as an example of unfair discrimination. At the same time, it will permit exceptions where a complete prohibition could place Canadian producers at a competitive disadvantage vis-a-vis foreign producers.
We think that the various legislative proposals I have just outlined will accomplish a number of things. The new objectives and principles will allow the government to provide a framework for the longer-term development of transportation policy. The reallocation of responsibilities between the minister, the Department of Transport and the Canadian Transport Commission will produce more effective policy development, program implementation and regulatory processes. The new freight rates provisions will lead to more equitable rates and better regulatory procedures.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would recall the words of the Minister of Transport in the policy statement of 1975 by reaffirming the historic role of transportation as an instrument of national purpose. We in the government believe that the major initiatives which have been taken to implement the new policy, and the package of legislative proposals introduced today, demonstrate clearly our continuing commitment to this historic role. It is a pleasure on my part to move second reading of this bill on behalf of my colleague, the Minister of

Transport, who as I explained is unavoidably absent from the House on important transportation business on the west coast. Naturally, he will be joining the debate on this bill in due course.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I also thank the House. These charts should be required reading for all those who are interested in and concerned about transportation. They clearly set out that we have a pretty efficient railway system in Canada today. They set out that the users of our railways pay 74 per cent of the cost. They set out clearly that the users of highways pay 64 per cent of the cost of the highways. The users of our civil aviation system, our airports and our airplanes, pay 31 per cent of the cost. The users of our marine services pay 19 per cent of the cost. When the minister says that we have heaped subsidy upon subsidy upon the railroad industry and that these subsidies have lead to inefficiency, we really must examine that very closely to find out in what way we are comparing the various modes of transportation.
I am not suggesting that in every part of Canada the railroads have operated efficiently, but generally speaking I think we can say they have, in spite of the actions of the government. We must also ask ourselves whether this legislation will make them more efficient, and I have to say no, it will not. The government has stated that it does not pretend that they will be more efficient. As outlined in clause 1 the government wants them to be an effective instrument of support for the achievement of national, regional, social, and economic objectives. The bill does not say that the government is prepared to pay or must pay for these social and regional objectives.
I am certain that both railways would like to think of themselves as being good corporate citizens and that they would respect the wishes of the government provided the government clearly stated somewhere in the legislation that it is prepared to pay these costs. Looking at that particularly, a few weeks ago the president of the CNR said, "We are going to sell those things which we manage, which we find a market for, and which we think are self-sustaining". The Minister of Transport made the same statement. But, Mr. Speaker, who will buy something that the government is saying must be operated as it decrees? I do not think that concept and this policy are compatible.
After reading the bill I ask myself where we are going in the area of transportation? Where is this legislation taking us? Will it solve the problems of the Snavely commission, the problems of the Hall commission, the problems of energy use in Canada today? I can only come to the conclusion that the bill falls far short of solving many of the problems that I see in the transportation industry today. It does not in any way set down guidelines which will motivate the government to direct the Canadian Transport Commission to do any of the things the government will have the power to do.
As I look at this great country of ours today I see we are deficient in oil and are likely to be so for many years. According to the Department of Energy, Mines and
March 1, 1977

Resources, 50 per cent of the oil consumed in Canada is used for transportation. But will this bill direct the transportation industry to conserve oil? In his speech the minister mentioned that we should bear that in mind, but the bill does not give any direction in this regard.
When we examine the user-pay concept we see that the people using the railroad pay the most. Perhaps we should reduce the subsidy to the inefficient users of oil and, if necessary, even increase the subsidy to the efficient users of oil to entice more tonnage to rail movement rather than truck movement. It is estimated that, using the same amount of oil, the railways haul four tons of goods whereas a truck hauls only one. The growth in truck tonnage in Canada has increased by about 17 per cent whereas the growth in rail tonnage has levelled off, or at best is going up only by 1 per cent or 2 per cent. A national transportation policy should give some direction in this regard.
We know that 60 per cent of the oil used in Canada is used by automobiles moving people in and out of the major population centres. Just before the bill was introduced the government announced the election promise of 1974 to spend $290 million to encourage the building of an electrical system for moving people in and out of the cities, a commuter transport system, was to be shelved.

speechtext: It will be resurrected for the next election.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
My hon. friend to my left suggests it will be resurrected at the next election. That would be an interesting resurrection. I do not think it would be believed; if it were, then the voters are more gullible than I thought.
I should like to see some indication in the bill that we are going to conserve energy through a transportation policy which would put us on the right road so that we could see a more efficient use of oil ten years ahead.
In his speech on June 11 the Minister of Transport suggested heavy subsidization. To date the heavy subsidization has been on Mirabel airport which we are told lost $50 million last year. The Minister of Finance tells us that most of that loss was interest charged on money. Mr. Speaker, who has ever borrowed money without paying interest? It is the cost of doing business. Why did they not consult the airlines before building Mirabel? If they had, perhaps the terminal would not have been designed the way it was or public transit vehicles used to move passengers from the terminal to the planes.
Many mistakes have been made in the past, and not by the transportation industry but by the bureaucrats. I have no axe to grind here. Mirabel exists and the best we can do is make good use of it, but I have recommended a couple of ways in which the service could be improved.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, the bureaucrats made most of the mistakes in our transportation policy, not the companies involved in each mode of transportation. Yet this bill gives more authority to the bureaucrats. Looking to the future as one interested in transportation, how can I say with confidence
National Transportation Act
that our system will be better and more efficient? I cannot, Mr. Speaker. If I knew for certain that the game of musical chairs mentioned by the president of the Canadian Trucking Association was not going to continue, and that sooner or later the Minister of Transport would be educated to the problems and adjust to the conditions that he meets in the area of transportation, I might have some confidence. But the musical chairs will continue, Mr. Speaker. The present Minister of Transport will not be minister very long. In fact if he keeps flying around in government airplanes to bonspiels and electioneering in provincial by-elections, his time as minister will probably be shortened very quickly.
As I travel across the country today, Mr. Speaker, I find people are upset and apprehensive about the future. Transportation plays a greater part in the life of Canadians than it does in any other country. In the United States transportation does not cost as much in goods consumed or produced, as in Canada. They have a great inland waterway which lowers transportation costs. We do not have such a good natural system. The countries of the European Common Market have the Rhine River which lowers their transportation costs; we have the St. Lawrence Seaway which only takes goods to half the country. Transportation will continue to play a very important part in the lives of all Canadians.
Instability in the transportation industry deepens the apprehensions we find in Canada today. Millions of dollars need to be spent on transportation-billions of dollars even to keep the present system functioning. Long range planning is essential, but how can we have that and spend the money necessary without any certainty that the policy which exists today will exist tomorrow? That is how quickly changes could be implemented through this legislation.
The governor in council can change that policy with a flick of the finger, and that is of concern to the industry. When we debated the original National Transportation Act in 1967 we said that the clauses having to do with captive shippers and the public interest would be inoperative. Events have proven us right. If a captive shipper faces a prohibitively high freight rate, he ought to be able to appeal quickly the decision setting that rate. The rapeseed case, which came under the public interest clause and which prairie provincial governments argued before the CTC, lasted two years.

speechtext: Four years.

speechtext:
I beg your pardon, four years. The CTC was seized of it for two years, and the government considered it for two years. That long delay did not bring salutary effects. We must establish a mechanism which will allow a more rapid disposition of appeals relating to the captive shipper and public interest sections. Lengthy appeals hurt the interest of those appealing. If the parties were concerned about the situation at the beginning of the appeal, imagine how concerned they were four years later when the matter was concluded. The damage was very great.

March 1, 1977
National Transportation Act
The Minister of Justice announced on behalf of the Minister of Transport the government's new passenger service policy. What is the government to get in return? Apparently the CPR is being taken off the hook. Part and parcel of the CPR's obligation, in return for its land and money grants for building the railway, is the provision of passenger service across Canada. But the present proposal will take the CPR off the hook, to the great delight of the CPR. What we are to get in return from the CPR the statement does not say. My part of Canada will be greatly interested in the deal, for we want to know what we are to get in return for concessions.
The Minister of Justice said that we are prepared to spend $30 million to improve passenger service between Quebec city and Montreal. I am puzzled about that $30 million matter. 1 have ridden the trains on the north side and the south side of the river, between Montreal and Quebec. I learned, for example, that last year 40,000 passengers travelled between Montreal and Quebec city on the CPR rails north of the river; something like 170,000 passengers travelled on the CNR rails south of the river, but 900,000 passengers travelled by bus last year between Montreal and Quebec. You would think the government would spend money on the most efficient mode of transportation, or the mode which most people choose. Unfortunately the government chooses to help the service which fewest people use. That is where the government will spend the $30 million.
I thought the CPR route must cover the shortest distance. However, on checking I found that the CPR's route between Montreal and Quebec city is the longest. I fail to understand the rationale of the bureaucrats who have devised this policy. 1 only use this example to show current thinking, and one could allude to many more unfortunate examples.
I raise the question of the Via Canada service. The deputy minister, Mr. Cloutier, not long ago said in the transport committee that the CPR is to be awarded the run between Montreal and Ottawa. That statement caused railway workers great concern. The minister's news release concerning Via Canada suggests that unions and workers are to be consulted and their views taken into consideration. But that is not what the deputy minister said when he told the committee that the CPR is to run the service between Montreal and Ottawa. The CPR runs two trains daily between Montreal and Ottawa, and the CNR six trains daily. Why award the service to the CPR, especially since this is a matter of great concern to CNR employees?
The minister suggested that when a Via Canada train runs over CNR tracks it will be pulled by a CNR engine, with a CNR crew; when it runs over CPR tracks it will be pulled by a CPR engine, with a CPR crew. The board of directors of the enterprise will be divided among representatives of the government, the CNR and the CPR. 1 say that conglomerate will not work. You will have jealousies as between both managements and as between managements and the Department of Transport.
Senior employees of the CNR have told me that the Department of Transport wants to run the railroads of this country.

They conclude that the department also wants to be involved in the running of the Via Canada service. 1 therefore say that there will be conflict among the three management groups. If the government wants to provide a rail passenger service, it should consider this matter carefully. It should not run the service under three managements. If it wants to set up a separate Crown corporation, let it set up a Canadian version of Amtrack to run our rail service. The corporation could get rights of way across Canada, and provide passenger service. This should not be done by the conglomerate. I say that its establishment is fraught with danger, jealousy, and anxiety. In this connection I commend to hon. members a reading of "The Wreck of the Penn Central", a book about the problems having to do with the amalgamation of the Central Railroad and the Pennsylvania Railroad in the United States. That amalgamation was unsuccessful. I submit that the proposal of the Minister of Transport will run into the same problem. It will not lead to the provision of the passenger services which Canada needs and deserves.
I do not see why two cities 200 miles apart cannot be provided with good, clean, frequent passenger service which people will use. The people would use a frequent rail service between Ottawa and Montreal. But they will not use it if the railways do not use the right equipment or if the trains do not run at the right times.
I regret that the bill proposes to give the government all kinds of power. Nowhere do I see provision for checks on that power. One cannot say that parliament checks the government's power; parliament has lost ability to control government expenditures. The CNR has not been before the transport committee for three or four years. Air Canada has not been before the committee for five or six years, and the CPR rarely appears before the committee. Our bureaucrats in Ottawa are studying everything, but nobody says in which direction we ought to go, and that is the trouble with the government, and with this legislation. This bill provides no direction for this country. No wonder the people of Canada are apprehensive about the future. The government has failed to provide leadership in all areas of its responsibilities, and this legislation fails in that regard as well.
People on the prairies are concerned about the Snavely commission, the Hall commission, the rationalization of branch lines, as well as the government's intent to raise tolls on the St. Lawrence Seaway. We built the Seaway and it should serve Canada. I agree it should pay the operating costs, but not the capital costs.
Massive expenditures have to be made on rails. This bill in no way suggests how that should be done. The CPR track between Calgary and Vancouver now operates at 100 per cent capacity. The CNR track from Edmonton to Vancouver is in terrible shape. It may be slightly better than the B.C. railroad, but not much.
This bill creates a climate of instability and insecurity. It does not encourage long range planning or capital expendi-
March 1, 1977

tures. I know there are some changes to the Railway Act. It will allow the railway to sell debentures in Canada and pay more than 6 per cent. CN recently sold debentures in Europe for more than 6 per cent. I am sure that if the Europeans knew of the uncertainty that exists within this rail policy, they would not be so quick to buy CN debentures.
I am sure this bill will go to committee and we in the opposition will have much more to say at that time. We will want to have the representatives of the CNR, CPR, the trucking associations, and maybe even of the marine association, appear before the transport committee to ensure us that they can operate and expand efficiently under this piece of legislation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I begin by endorsing some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner). We have been waiting many years for a significant revision of the National Transportation Act, the Railway Act, and the transportation policy of the government. However, on the day the bill is called for debate in parliament, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is not here. We on this side fully appreciate that he has to be in different parts of Canada from time to time on official business. However, if that takes priority over being in this place to introduce this vital legislation, or announcing the Via rail passenger corporation, the Minister of Transport is being derelict in his duty and has insulted the members of this House of Commons. Like the hon. member for Crowfoot, I suspect he is more likely in and around Saskatoon and Prince Albert messing around in a couple of provincial by-elections.
I want to say on behalf of the New Democratic Party that we will oppose this "user pay" legislation on the grounds that it endorses the notion of commercial viability as opposed to the concept of transportation as a public utility.
This legislation makes user pay the basis of the government's transportation policy. We take exception to the notion that the public interest should be denied in favour of competition and commercial viability. That is what got us into this transportation mess and has kept us there since the early 1900's, the concept of commercial viability and competition in transportation. Now the government restores the very kind of policy that maintains and strengthens the kind of transportation legislation that got us into this trouble.
A policy that relies on those two concepts, commercial viability and competition, will in effect, as it has done up until now, deny national, regional, social, and economic goals that this country should have. It will deny equity and accessibility to people who live in the outlying areas of Canada. It will shift the burden of cost of transportation, previously shared by the nation as a whole, on to those least able to shoulder the burden.
We submit that transportation must be treated as a public utility because it is something that everyone must use. A comprehensive and fair transportation policy should incorporate the following principles.
National Transportation Act
Our major modes of transportation should be publicly owned, operated, and accountable to the people and to parliament. Service to the public should take precedence over profitability. Every member of this House knows that all modes of transportation have to be subsidized. There is not a single mode of transportation that pays its own way. This is even more the case in a country like Canada than those countries which are smaller in geography and have densely settled populations.
In a country like ours which has a large geography, northern climate, widely scattered population, the transportation system cannot function properly when it is on the basis of private enterprise, competition, and commercial viability. The former minister of transport once said that competition does not work in transportation. It was not a New Democrat who said that but a Liberal.
We believe the transportation system must serve as an instrument to achieve national, regional, social and economic goals. I am sure members on all sides will agree with that. In fact words similar to that are in this bill.
We also believe a transportation policy must have equality of treatment and accessibility to the various modes of transportation, no matter where in this country people may live or where the goods are processed or manufactured.
People in this country have always been discriminated against because of where they live. Processors and manufacturers have been discriminated against because of where they have been located. Our transportation system has never provided equality of treatment. Central Canada, with the most dense population, for the free enterprise reasons we have had for the past 110 years, has had the best quality transportation services because that is where the main market is located. Users of transportation in central Canada get the best rates and fares. The rest of the country has been faced with inadequate service, discriminatory rates, impossible fares, and schedules that are unreasonable. This legislation does not provide equity and reasonable accessibility to all Canadians, no matter where they live in this country.
An efficient transportation system should be developed replacing competition with co-ordination and integration, so that the most appropriate mode of transportation is assigned its given task. I realize that some of these objectives are stated in the new legislation, but the government's commitment to these announced goals is expressed in terms so tentative, so limited, and so hesitant as to call in question the sincerity and strength of its conversion.
The National Transportation Act of 1967, based on the MacPherson Royal Commission, assumed that competition would guide the organization of transportation.
The former minister of transport, Mr. Marchand, had some second thoughts about the principles of competition. In his policy statement of 1975 he said:

March 1, 1977
National Transportation Act
... if you look at the size of this country and the distribution of its population you will see that you cannot have a transportation network which is economic everywhere; you cannot have an economic system of transportation to service the north, for example, or to service those regions of the country where the population is very thin. You cannot have an ecomomic system for regions which are remote from the centre.
In spite of these brave words, the actual policy tabled in June 1975 reflected little change from the policy which Mr, Marchand said in 1974 resulted in the transportation policy of this country being "in a mess".
In the new transportation policy of June 1975 competition and commercial viability remained enshrined as the guiding principles of transportation policy in Canada. Either Mr. Marchand had lost a major battle with his cabinet colleagues, or he was less than sincere in his public suggestions of drastic changes in transportation policies in Canada.
Much of the substance of this legislation is vague and general. Considering the minister's past statements on the Crowsnest pass grain rates and rail passenger service, one might be thankful that there were no specific references to these last remaining benefits. But make no mistake, the minister has specific intentions and this legislation will give him the power to carry his "user pay" policy to the painful extreme.
In his news release of Jan. 27, 1977, the minister said the amendments to the transportation legislation in Bill C-33 will provide the Minister of Transport with the legislative means to implement the transportation policy as announced in June, 1975. The June, 1975, policy states that the user shall pay for transportation services:
Generally, where transportation services are mature, the users should be expected to pay for the costs of providing the services.
As far as I am concerned, this means the people of western Canada can say, "There goes the statutory grain rate!" It also means that those in the maritime provinces can say, "There go the maritime freight rate subsidies!" In my opinion they have already been sold out by the four premiers of the Atlantic provinces-two Liberals and two Tories. I don't know what the minister said or did to them, but to my mind they have sold out; they have sold out their own people.
What are the mature transportation services referred to and for which the user is to pay? The policy states that movements in mature transport markets include: eastern forest products, northern Ontario resources, Quebec-Labrador ore, western bulk products, and B. C. forest products.
What about passenger transport, which most directly affects people? The June, 1975, policy states:
A more balanced approach to passenger service is required giving consideration to an eventual objective of full commercial viability, including recovery of infrastructure costs, except in remote areas, where traffic volumes may be inadequate and assistance may be required.
Carrying the user-pay policy to a conclusion means that only the rich or those on expense accounts will be able to travel. It means that those who live outside the central corridor will pay even higher charges than those who live along it. It means continued discrimination against Canadians based on where they happen to live.
[Mr. Benjamin.)
The bill is bad in principle because it strengthens and enhances the principles which were previously in the policy. There is no fundamental change in that policy. In fact, it is made worse. To apply the user-pay principle in a country such as ours would jeopardize the sale of our grain overseas. It would jeopardize the success of industries which could and should be started up in the prairie provinces and in the maritimes. Our transportation must have a relatively neutral effect upon the cost of travel or freight if we are to compete effectively either in markets overseas or in domestic markets which are far from the seat of production.
Parcelling out the national transportation system into commercially viable operations and those which are not, leaving the parts which lose money on the backs of the taxpayers, means eliminating the opportunity to cross-subsidize. Crosssubsidization is one of the ways of sharing the cost of transportation. Profits from operations in a densely populated area can help pay for losses incurred in a sparsely populated part of the country. But, no. This government, with the support of the Tories, wants private enterprise to keep the profitable part, letting them make all the money they can, while allowing the cost of the unprofitable part to be borne by those who use the services and by the taxpayers generally through subsidies. And the people who own the profitable parts of the system will be able to laugh all the way to the bank at the expense of our nationhood.
I agree that users should help pay for the operations of our transport system. The important question then is, what is an appropriate user charge? It seems to me that two things have to be taken into consideration here; (1) the cost of providing the service; (2) the value of the service to the national or regional interest and the goals of equity and accessibility.
The user charges for public transport should be set at a level to render the service accessible. In many cases this level would be below the cost of providing the service.
I suppose that the government's reneging on the promise of $300 million aid to urban transit is in line with its user pay philosophy in transportation. Clearly though, here is a case where the value of the service should be given priority. The cost benefit of that transit aid would include lower energy consumption, decreased need for new highways, reduced pollution, and decreased burden of automobile accidents.
Freight rates for products of our regional industries should be set at a level to give them access to the larger market of the whole Canadian people instead of the restricted market of the region. In many cases this toll would be less than the cost of providing the service.
The nation as a whole should share the costs of transportation because the nation as a whole benefits from it. It allows Canada through its Canadian grain producers to sell grain outside our borders in competition with other exporting nations which raise their grain close to the sea coast or which have access to inland waterways. Without those statutory rates, Canada ceases to become a competitor in the world market for export grains.
March 1, 1977

When the minister suggests that possibly the benefits of those rates should go to the grain producers in some other way, that is the most nonsensical, stupid, and inefficient method of sharing the cost of transportation that one can imagine. It would be an administrative nightmare, if nothing else. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, officials in Industry, Trade and Commerce trying to sort out all the way bills and each farmer's entitlement to some form of direct subsidy out of 180,000 grain permit holders, several million carload lots or partial carload lots? It is simply outrageous. Surely it is simpler and more sensible to continue to pay whatever is the deficit in the cost of transporting grain direct to the transporters, with the requirement that they maintain their trackage, service and equipment.
I do not believe that either of the railways, singly or combined, have the financial capacity to raise the necessary capital to rebuild their systems. This will require massive capital funding from the nation as a whole. Neither the railroad nor private enterprise and financial institutions will ever be willing, and in many cases are unable, to carry that kind of funding.
I should like to discuss some of the objectives and principles contained in this bill specifically, since we are debating the bill on second reading. We take exception to certain provisions within the bill, specifically the proposed section 3(2)(d), which provides that "competition within and between modes of transport should be encouraged where economic and technical factors permit." It was this very kind of competition which got us into the mess we are in in regard to all this nonsense about DC-9's, DC-8's and 727's flying 120 miles from Ottawa to Montreal. Both Air Canada and CP Air have been losing their shirts on that run during the last three years. It is inefficient and wasteful, particularly in terms of energy costs, to continue to do this. It is no quicker than a fast train. In fact at some times of the day it is not as quick as a fast train. But the government wants to maintain the mythology of competition between modes of transportation. This is what has got us into trouble.
The notion of competition in transportation conflicts with our advocacy that transportation should be operated as a public utility. I want to quote what was said by the former leader of our party, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas). In the debate on the National Transportation Act in 1966 he had this to say:
We will be leaning on a broken reed if we depend on competition to keep transportation rates at a price that is fair and reasonable . . . What about the areas where there are no alternative forms of transportation? The areas in the maritimes, in northern Quebec, northern Ontario and on the prairies . .. These regions will not have the kind of competition which would keep freight rates at a reasonable figure ... I greatly fear that the removal of restraints and restrictions on the railways with reference to freight rates will mean that regions of Canada are going to pay the shot, and that some of the burden which heretofore had been borne by all the people of Canada is going to fall upon those areas of Canada which can least afford to carry this burden.
Of this legislation, Mr. Speaker, exactly the same thing can be said. If it were logical to have competing railways and
National Transportation Act
competing airlines, it would be equally logical to have competing sewer and water systems, highways, telephone lines, electric lines, fire brigades, police departments-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: And post offices.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Yes, and post offices. That would be ridiculous. If anyone seriously suggested that kind of competition, they would be locked up. For the government to suggest that kind of competition in transportation, it too deserves to be locked up.
When we talk about transportation under a utility that is publicly owned and controlled, publicly accountable to parliament, with a public utilities board or whatever method you want to use, it is not some socialist dogma. This is what has been done with transportation systems all over the world in countries of all political persuasions; it is not just some NDP or socialist ideology. Private enterprise governments and several variations thereof did this decades ago. For example, under Conrad Adenauer during the 1950's and 1960's the West Germans reorganized their transportation system. So did the Dutch, Belgians, Scandinavians, and French.
I do not completely agree with the comments of the hon. member for Crowfoot in his comments about the Via rail passenger corporation. The trans-European express is run by a separate corporation which owns all its own equipment. It uses different railroad and crews as it passes through five or six European countries. I suggest we could use some of the ideas under that system because it works very well. They are not all adaptable to the Canadian scene, but certainly we do not disagree in principle with the idea of a national passenger transportation Crown corporation, though it is second best; we would rather see all railroads and air lines brought under a national Crown corporation.
We suggest it is not logical, sensible or efficient to have competition and commercial viability in transportation because this will continue to discriminate against people in this country because of where they live. Competition between modes of transportation misallocates resources and wastes them by making inappropriate use of the various modes. It is just nonsense to have trains stopping every five miles; that is a job for buses. It is equally nonsensical to have planes make 200 to 300 mile trips. We are not using the various modes of transportation in a sensible and efficient manner.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO STIPULATE "BREAKDOWN PRINCIPLE" SOLE BASIS FOR DIVORCE
speechtext:
that Bill C-224, an act respecting divorce, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the bill which I am putting before the House is based upon the substitution, as grounds for divorce, of the concept of the breakdown of marriage in place of the present concept, which is largely dependent upon proof of what are known as matrimonial offences.
There are two major theories on what should be the grounds for divorce. The first is that divorce should be based on fault; that is to say, that a court should determine that one of the parties to the marriage has committed a matrimonial offence, such as adultery, cruelty, desertion and so forth. The second is that when in fact marriage no longer exists for its basic purpose of enabling the parties to live together in harmony and there is no hope of reconciliation, then the marriage should be terminated. That is the breakdown theory which I have advocated. For a long time these two principles have contended with each other. In 1967 and 1968 the Canadian parliament chose the former course, and in substance our present act is based upon the concept of the matrimonial offence, the fault of one of the parties who, if at fault, cannot secure relief himself or herself.
When the matter was discussed by the joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate at the time of the passing of the previous bill, which is now our present act, a minority, which included the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin), the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), Mr. Gordon Aiken who was then the hon. member for Parry Sound, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), and myself, urged the necessity for the broader reform, namely, the concept of marriage breakdown to replace the existing grounds of divorce. This proposal was fully developed in a report made to the Archbishop of Canterbury in England by a distinguished group of churchmen, lawyers, doctors and sociologists. Also, it was embodied in a book called "Putting Asunder".
The concept of breakdown of marriage as grounds for divorce was then supported by the United Church of Canada, the Anglican Church of Canada, the National Council of Women, the Canadian Mental Health Association, the Canadian Jewish Congress, and the Canadian Committee on the Status of Women. Now it has received powerful reinforcement by a report of the Law Reform Commission of Canada. I think it is an interim report of that commission which recommends that breakdown of marriage be the sole ground for divorce.
I have incorporated in Bill C-224 the main provisions recommended by the Law Reform Commission and the proposals in "Putting Asunder". Before dealing with the provisions of the bill in detail, I should like to make clear the basic point of view which the proposal sets forth. It is an acceptance of the centrality of marriage as the most important institution in society, linked as it is with the whole concept of the family. I have spoken of the centrality of marriage. There are many of us, among whom I am one, who speak also of the sanctity of marriage as being more than a merely human institution, although it is indeed a great human institution. If I may be permitted a more personal note, I speak with conviction on this subject through personal experience of a happy marriage and a happy family life.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Turner).]
