subsubtopic: MEASURE TO STIPULATE "BREAKDOWN PRINCIPLE" SOLE BASIS FOR DIVORCE
speechtext:
It would not be a very happy marriage if she could coerce me in what I say in the House.
Marriage has been defined as the voluntary union for life of one man and one woman to the exclusion of all others. I accept this definition and I regard the concept as one of indisolubility, and the purpose of this legislation which 1 am bringing forth is to advance and not diminish this concept. But it must be recognized by all of us that the hope and expectations of many for permanent union are dashed. Many marriages break down, and when they do serious problems arise, not only for the immediate parties but for the children of the marriage.
It is necessary, therefore, for the state to recognize the existence of the breakdown of marriage and make provisions for the legal ending of what morally is no longer reality. Indeed, some marriages are sources of strife in themselves. The approach of the matrimonial offences theory sets up barriers, and creates an adversary process in the courts which is both expensive and painful. Husbands and wives are often contending with each other. The present system creates these adversary procedures which, as I said, are expensive, provoke bitterness, and encourage-I say this advisedly-adultery, collusion, and sometimes perjury. The present system provides no effective means of encouraging reconciliation. When I say this I speak as one who has had some experience in the courts on these matters.
The present Bill C-224 defines the courts which have jurisdiction and provides that a petition for divorce may be presented when the marriage is broken down and there is no reasonable possibility of reconciliation.
When the husband and wife have lived apart and separate for one year, the marriage is deemed to have broken down. A duty is imposed upon the court to have special regard for the children of the marriage and to consider the possibility of reconciliation. Where in any stage of the proceedings reconciliation appears possible, the court may, with consent of the parties, adjourn the proceedings so that reconciliation can be worked at by the parties, or a person qualified in marriage counselling may be nominated to aid in the reconciliation. The court may refuse a decree if it would be unduly harsh to either spouse or prejudicially affect the making of reasonable arrangements for either spouse and for the custody, care and maintenance of the children of the marriage as might be necessary in the circumstances.
It is sometimes said that this is equivalent to divorce by consent, or divorce at the unilateral will of any of the parties. This is a misreading of the legislation. The proposed act provides that the court cannot grant a decree until two years have passed since the day of the marriage. This would prevent rushing to the divorce courts almost immediately after the
Divorce
marriage without time for proper consideration. There are cases now where divorce is granted on the basis of the committing of a single act of adultery. Under the breakdown concept the commission of a single act of adultery would not in itself justify a divorce unless it had led to the breakdown of the marriage and the breakdown of the reality behind the marriage.
It cannot be too much emphasized that the present system frequently brings the courts into contempt. The proposal we make would remove from the courts the sordid story of adultery and fabrication of evidence which are all too common at present.
In order to make this legislation work, it is clear that a different form of inquiry into the background is required, and we believe that there are those who are trained or could be trained in this field and who could report to the court on the facts of the breakdown of the marriage or whether there was a hope of reconciliation.
It may be asked what, in effect, is the breakdown of marriage. It is a condition or situation in which the life-long union of husband and wife is beyond hope of recovery; where the institution is not honoured, and human happiness and welfare are not being served, and the marriage has become a shell and ought to be declared non-existent.
It is our view that it is not divorce that destroys families, but bad marriages. As the Law Commission report says, the common assumption that liberal divorce laws breed irresponsibility must be challenged. We believe the number of people who marry and divorce without reason constitute only a fraction of our married population. If constructive solutions are to be sought, the answer lies not in our divorce laws but in family life education and marriage counselling.
Social welfare programs that reflect reasonable family policies and promote family cohesion must be developed to deal with such extrinsic facts as unemployment, sickness, and inadequate housing that place undue strain on the stability of marriage and the family unit.
I realize that the great objection many people have to this legislation, consciously or unconsciously, lies in the fact that it breaks new ground, but as the Law Reform Commission report indicates, the trend throughout the civilized world is to introduce marriage breakdown as the sole ground for divorce.
I urge this House to take a stand in favour of a more humane, more rational, and more civilized approach to the problem of broken homes and marriages. Many of the churches and other institutions I have mentioned, as well as the Law Reform Commission, have shown the way. It is up to us as legislators to have the courage to follow this way even if it is to some of us a new concept.

and I appreciate his introducing this bill in this House. Again, however, I fear that the whole approach to the vast social problems we have with regard to matrimonial law and law involving children's rights is being corrected in a patchwork fashion. I wish the whole of our law could be repaired in one piece of legislation suitable for the society of the late twentieth century.
However, I support this bill completely, and I congratulate the hon. member for Greenwood for his persistence in trying to eliminate, once and for all, the terribly destructive adversary system and in trying to correct the tragedy and pain of marriage failure. Our laws have compounded the destructiveness which exists in the very private matter of marriage breakdown. I agree that marriage breakdown must be the only and absolute ground for dissolving marriages.
I think our matrimonial laws must have been written by self-serving men. Men must take the blame because they authorized all laws, civil and secular, and now we are trying to catch up and correct those laws.
Laws with regard to matrimonial affairs are obsolete, as are many of today's laws. They complicate matters rather than add to the peace and joy of today's life. Our matrimonial laws are simplistic; they are black and white. They must be black and white because people in courts do not seem to be able to think in any other way. It must either be black-white, right or wrong, angel or devil, but no gray or shaded area. That is too subtle for some adjudicators of law to understand.
When the whole tragedy of love going sour occurs, we must have someone to blame. However, both sides could very well be blamed and the whole matter resolved without added trauma. It is an anathema in the late twentieth century to have courts determine who is the matrimonial culprit in an unsuccessful marriage. It is like walking in cold to the middle of a street riot and trying to find the single one who started it.
When the law was changed from the single ground of adultery, the halls outside and inside the court rooms on divorce day in Vancouver, where I worked, were rather like a subdued pilgrimage of children-drawn, pale, and waiting to join that terrible internecine war between their parents. They were obliged to tell a complete stranger, the judge, in a totally strange world of black-robed people how bad, cruel, and brutal one parent was, and how the other in goodness suffered.
One parent is good, the other bad, and child must tell this to the court. I saw this over and over again with despair, because the amendment which corrected the law only made it worse. Children had to testify-under oath in many cases-for one parent against the other. They had to tell family secrets. They had to tell shameful secrets which are terribly disturbing to youngsters. They had to tell what went on between their parents in the privacy of their home.
Internecine war must be the crudest and most vicious of all wars, and in this war the children are forced to the front line among all the bullets. They never forget. I have known children who have grown to adulthood who never forgot that they lived in that no-man's land of their parents' war, and for the

rest of their lives some of them blamed themselves for causing the marriage breakups.
As immature and chauvinistic as the one ground of adultery was, it was better than what happened when blame became broader and had to be proved in law. However, both laws, the old one with regard to adultery and the new one which includes many grounds, were designed by medieval minds, and to say the least they are inappropriate in Canada in 1977.
Worst of all these laws damage all parties who must participate in these sordid charades. I am not saying I want freedom or licentiousness in our human relations, and certainly no one was more vocal than I in damning the type of behaviour which developed in the latter half of the 1960's. Lifestyles during that period deteriorated to a point where anything was right. Morality and discipline in human behaviour was sneered at. Marriage was looked on as a joke, as old fashioned. Doing one's own thing was acceptable and was even touted by some impressive voices from the media and from academe, who also wanted to do their own thing in sex perversion and drugs. They touted this philosophy so that they could have their own gratification.
Marriage and an essential commitment of one human being to another, a lifelong commitment, make people strong, if they can work out that complex partnership. Certainly it is the safest and most ideal framework in which to raise and nurture children. Strong human beings come out of strong marriages, especially those which are not only strong but happy as well. It takes remarkable women and remarkable men to raise children successfully alone without support.
It is in this regard that I say the state should be active, rather than in intervention in the breakup of marriages, in helping people to prepare for marriage and to succeed in marriage. Many have raised children alone quite successfully, but if marriage fails the danger to children should not be increased further by the need to turn one parent into an offender before the law; to force one parent to be bad and to leave the mark of that bad parent forever in the memory of the child. In all likelihood that child will identify with the "evil" of the parent, and somehow believe forever that they, being of that same cloth, are also "evil".
Partnerships break up because it is humanly impossible to have total perfection and compatibility in human relationships. Those which are successful survive because one partner is willing to compromise, to suffer hurt, and to accept less than perfection. On rare occasions each party will adapt to the foibles of the other and love the weaknesses because they love the complete human person they vowed jointly to love, honour and cherish through all life. Some stay together, however, in mutual tolerance, perhaps even in indifference and, of course, there are numerous people who stay together in pain.
But to have the adversary system, the fault system, and to have to go before a court of law to dissolve marriages is absolutely beyond conception in this day and age. Among those who set the original design have been men who perhaps never lived in marriage. Some were men of the church who were celibate, preserving their world for men.
March 1, 1977

When a marriage is irretrievably broken, and all attempts between the two people and the family involved fail, the state is best served if the psychological and physical battering which follows marriage breakdown and precedes divorce does not happen. Desertion and abandonment have been the solution for some. There are even instances in which a partner seeks escape quickly by murder, foolishly preferring it to the slow anguish of divorce and all the public recriminations.
Love cannot be rehabilitated once contempt, boredom or hate take over. The progression from love to hate can be very speedy, and anyone who dreams he can cure a broken love affair or a broken marriage is certainly in dreamland. People like that have seen too much of Hollywood of the early days and too much of the bad television of today. If somewhere between those extreme poles of love and hate, a final decision could be made rationally, without the rancour, without the violence that too often is as passionate as the early love, both the principals and the children would be safer emotionally and physically.
As it is now, children are too often used for the barter in matrimonial trade-offs. In exchange for money-the maintenance that was not paid-the husband is allowed to have the children for a week end or at Christmastime. Christmas is the popular time for barter. The children soon become wise to a most devious human technique to achieve desires, or even power-manipulating one parent against the other for their personal gain.
The reasons I agree with the hon. for Greenwood are many. The law must be changed to forever end this charade we call divorce and the seemingly inevitable internecine war that so often accompanies it and that so sorely damages the principals, but most of all injures the children who are our future.
There are many cynical lines about marriage and divorce such as: divorce is like matrimony, a fellow has to go through it three or four times before he knows how. There are many lines that can be quoted but, Mr. Speaker, it is a serious business. When marriage breaks it is the most tragic business of all. There are many jokes about it, but it is the tragedy of our time that there is so much divorce which clogs the courts and destroys families and children.
In Vancouver there was a sanctimonious fraud on the bench, now deceased. I should not speak ill of the dead. Nonetheless, I cannot forget how he lined up all the women after a day of divorce hearings, usually a Friday, and lectured them on religion, their duty to their children and their duty to their now departed, divorced mate. It was deplorable, but it indicated the power tripping that I have seen on the part of some lawyers- and a few judges-in the tragedy of divorce.
One lawyer who specializes in divorce does everything to degrade a woman when she comes to his office. He calls her a tramp, a whore, spewing out epithets laced with four-letter words. A psychiatrist might suggest he nurtures his sexual inadequacies by using four letter words over and over again even though the woman is a total stranger. The women come
Divorce
away degraded, beaten, with their already devastated selfesteem totally eliminated. However, the woman endures this despicable tirade because the lawyer has the reputation of winning, and of taking all for his client. But this is all part of what can happen in the long drawn out divorce process, where a lawyer can play around with blame.
To put it simply, perpetrating matrimonial offences in law does many things. First, it damages the children. Second, it forces children to become the catalyst in the court battle; third, as John Barrymore once said, "a paper napkin never returned from a laundry nor love from a trip to the law courts". Fourth, reconciliation by court or by law is impossible; it cannot succeed unless the partners want it to. Fifth, marriage in quiet despair and constant battle makes people less able to function in the general fabric of society and serve in their jobs, occupations or professions. When marriage breakdown occurs, that is devastating by itself. Why then is it necessary for the state to add to the pain of adversary law and matrimonial offence, the court process in which both men and women are strangers in this strange land?
My sixth point is that battles between man and wife are absolutely confidential. What rationale can there be for going public? Did lawyers create the adversary system to keep lawyers rich or perhaps for justification to force these people into the open for the gratification of a society that cannot change what has happened in the privacy of their home? As Oscar Levant put it; "My first wife divorced me on the grounds of incompatibility. Besides I think she hated me." Sometimes one wonders who gave these people more pleasure; the clergyman who married them or the judge who divorced them.
The seventh point is one that is much in the news but has probably happened throughout the century although we have just become aware of it, that is the plight of the battered woman and child. They are no doubt the victims of marriage breakdown. No person should have to come to court to obtain relief from battering in marriage. Nor should she have to prove no fault to escape from such a horrible situation. Cruelty, a ground in law, should be accepted as absolute in such cases and should not have to be debated in a courtroom. As one woman said, "Yes, my grounds were cruelty; he tried to kill me several times."
Human failure is devastating enough without having to expose it in court. It should be resolved quietly, by mutual consent, registering an end to marriage with vital statistics. That is enough. If it is not done by mutual consent, the individual-the parties-will go their own way anyhow and the venom in one marriage will spread to other marriages and other homes.
Adultery and the use of prostitution is another way of solving the problem. Perhaps the state should concern itself with nurturing the marriage and if it fails, let the parties be free to suffer the failure with a certain amount of dignity and with minimal pain.
Everything should be done to prevent divorce by serving and preparing for good marriage. It is the most important partner-

ship undertaken-certainly more important than those based only on making money. Think of all the laws we have now to protect corporations and business when making money is the prime objective-school for eight, 12 or 20 years to prepare for that, but there is no preparation for the most important duty a human being is ever to undertake-marriage. If the partnership fails, there is no restoring it. The adversary attempt at reconstruction is sheer madness. As usual, it is the imagined remedy of men and lawyers. Women have not been active long enough in the policy-making areas of society to clean up the act, but maybe it will be a different world now that they are becoming more involved.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO STIPULATE "BREAKDOWN PRINCIPLE" SOLE BASIS FOR DIVORCE
speechtext:
The people who constructed our social order, made it too complex, too unjust-an impossible framework in which humans must strive to live in peace.
I am afraid lawyers must take the blame for complicating our lives almost beyond endurance. It is as though the whole of our lives was designed to make lawyers rich and make us fearful. As you know, a man will joyfully pay a lawyer $500 for untying the knot of wedlock, but he begrudges a clergyman $50 for tying it. That is how little regard the man has for a commitment to marriage, and how speedily he wants freedom. It is true now of women as well because they are economically freer to escape the bondage of a bad marriage. It also explains why lawyers are richer than clergymen.
Our whole society seems geared to litigation and is routed through the courts. Marriages should never have to go that way, and certainly children should not have to be the arbiters of the good and bad of their parents.
The male rules for morality nurtured immorality and kept women tied to a separate set of rules for male convenience and service. Thus, if a man engages in adultery he is a gay blade; a woman who becomes involved is a tramp-a whore. If a man engages the services of a prostitute, the woman is charged with the offence while the man goes free. His name is not even recorded in the crime report. The man, who should be the complainant, of course cannot complain because his name would go on the record and his reputation be destroyed. No male who wrote the law would ever want that to happen to one of his. But it does not matter about the woman. Chivalry? No! male self-preservation-by law.
Divorce is of the same design, but now that women have been freed economically by their own ability to make a living, maybe the double standard will diminish.
When marriage fails there is no question that there cannot be recovery for that marriage. I have seen attempted reconciliations but they have never worked. They have merely delayed the inevitable, or the couples and the children have lived together in silent and often violent despair. Many ended up in mental hospitals or certainly as disturbed people.
[Mrs. Holt.)
Love can be a terrible weakening process. After it has started to deteriorate, it can leave its victims physically and emotionally debilitated. We are so easily victimized if we love too much but, worse, devastated if we hate too much. To put it in the words of Helen Rowland, a columnist and author who seemed to have first-hand experience, a grass widow was the angel a man loved, the human being he married, and the devil he divorced. She also described love as the quest, marriage the conquest, and divorce the inquest.
I would wish for our society that which the hon. member for Greenwood proposes-that the inquest be quiet, peaceful, and without search for someone to blame. The litigation route is destructive.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO STIPULATE "BREAKDOWN PRINCIPLE" SOLE BASIS FOR DIVORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite some of the things the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) said about men and lawyers, and that was an arguable point which I could debate with her, I must say that, generally, I agreed with her approach and with the approach of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin).
I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway that the law was made by men. Originally it was made by so-called celibates. The ecclesiastical law for many years was the foundation of our divorce law. In mediaeval ages, and even later, the divorce courts were ecclesiastical courts. Henry VIII changed all that; he had a much more clear-cut way of getting rid of his wives-if I can make a pun. I remember reading a book about some of the oddities of the ecclesiastical law. According to that book, in the early days of the United Kingdom when a man took a wife he took her property and he also took her debts. But if he married her in her shift, he did not have to take her debts. I am sure the hon member for Vancouver-Kingsway will appreciate the dilemma of the woman in ancient days. She had to choose between getting dressed to kill, getting married in a beautiful white wedding dress and letting her husband pay her debts, and getting married in her shift and not letting her husband pay her debts.
I remember, when I came back from overseas after the last war, that I did a lot of divorce work. I was not happy to do it, did not like it, but it was work which had to be done. Many divorces arose because young people had married hastily in wartime and then parted quickly because one of the partners was in the armed services. When they met again they both discovered that their marriage partners were completely different from what they had envisaged. I did many divorces between 1946 and 1950. The divorce rate was fantastically high, compared with what it had been up to that period in our history.
I remember being in a building-it was not really a courtroom-and seeing the presiding judge grant 12 decrees nisi in one hour. Each divorce took five minutes on average. The lawyers knew it was a farce. It was all laid on. The marriage certificate was produced, there were photographs, proofs of service, proofs of the existence of children, evidence to estab-
March 1, 1977

lish that there was no collusion, evidence to establish adultery and, bingo, that was it. It took five minutes.
I remember the judge having difficulty with a newly minted barrister who was a little embarrassed at having to bring such evidence forward. The judge said to him, "Come on, hurry up. Adultery may be very pleasant to commit, but 1 have sat here for three days listening to such evidence, and listening to adultery cases is not my idea of a good time." He said, "Prove adultery, and let us end this case." That happened in a building in my town which had been turned into a courthouse. Actually, the building had been used before as a United Church. The new courthouse was being built at the time. One of the two clients I had in this series of divorce cases looked around him and said, "Mr. Baldwin, is this the old United Church building?" I said, "Yes, it is." He said, "My God, that's where I was married." Even though I believe in freedom of information I will not tell you what I charged him for his divorce, but I can tell you that it cost him much more to get his divorce than it had cost him to get married.
I agree with what has been said. I can say, on my experience as a lawyer, as a member of parliament and private citizen, that the reliance on fraud, perjury, hypocrisy, and all the nastiness involved in using the adversary system to prove adultery, bestiality or any of the other grounds which originally were grounds for divorce, is simply criminal in the eyes of society. Yet we persisted in this country for many years in accepting such grounds as the only basis for divorce. Our governments were far, far behind the people.
Finally in 1965 or 1966 a joint committee was set up under the excellent chairmanship of the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) and Senator Roebuck, a distinguished member of the other place. That committee sat either for one year and a half or two years, heard many witnesses, read the book "Putting Asunder" which had been prepared at the instance of the Archbishop of Canterbury following an inquiry by a judge of the high court of England, a bishop, and one or two other people, and made some good recommendations. They did not go as far as the hon. member for Greenwood and I and others wanted them to go. On the basis of what we had read, heard and seen, we believed then, as we both do now, that marriage breakdown, properly established, should be the basic ground for the dissolution of marriage. But the committee did not go that far. It went half way to meet us.
I can recall that the hon. member for Greenwood, 1 and one or two other members of the day went to 24 Sussex Drive to see the then prime minister, Mr. Pearson. We proposed that marriage breakdown should constitute at least a major cause, or major ground for the dissolution of marriages. Mr. Pearson was quite receptive to our idea and said he would discuss it with the minister of justice of that day.
Ultimately the new divorce bill was presented in this House, either in 1966 or 1967. We found that not only had the then minister of justice not gone as far as we wanted, but he and his officials had not even gone as far as the committee had recommended. Try as we would, we could not persuade the then minister of justice to change his mind. I suggested at the
Divorce
time that, because of his attitude on social matters, politically the then minister of justice was slightly to the left of Ghengis Khan. That minister of justice became our present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), Mr. Speaker. I have since come to the conclusion that he stands about even with Ghengis Khan.
Putting nasty politics to one side, I wish to repeat what the hon. member for Greenwood put forward: the adversary system is not the system to use in the dissolution of marriages. Adultery, cruelty and desertion are consequences, or the fallout, rather than the cause of dissolution of marriage. A time may come during a marriage when only the ashes are left, when there is no spark to revive. When that happens it is futile to compel two adult people to go through this forlorn process of manufacturing or creating evidence of adultery and all the rest of it. I think it is wrong. That is why I like what the hon. member for Greenwood has proposed in his bill, because it would provide that a divorce may be granted when there is no reasonable possibility of reconciliation. Generally that does not happen today. If, under the adversary system, the petitioner establishes adultery or such other cause as is contemplated by the act, as far as the court is concerned, it is over. It is finished. The judge is not required to make any investigation into the question of reconciliation. That is quite important.
An experienced trial judge, with long knowledge of human nature derived from sitting on the bench, is probably very capable of determining whether the marriage is completely shot, whether it is kaput, or whether there is prospect of some reconciliation. The mandate to be laid upon a judge by this bill is much better than the situation which exists today.
When people use adultery as a ground for divorce, they often go right through the trial without even a hint of reconciliation being considered. The same applies to the question of children, compensation or alimony, as the case may be.
I go along with the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. It would be excellent if jurisdiction could be combined with the whole matter of matrimonial life and the custody of children in one area or court. Obviously you are not going to get the kind of changes to the British North America Act which would bring this about. However, through the use of delegated authority the attorneys general of the federal and provincial governments could in due course consider this. Through the use of delegated power in the legislation, it is quite legal to transfer to one court or group, call it what you will, the right to deal with all aspects of matrimonial life including, where necessary, dissolution of the marriage, custody of children, and awarding of alimony and maintenance. This would be highly desirable.
I could speak on this for a considerable length of time but I think I have made it clear where I stand. Unless the hon. member for Greenwood has been more persuasive with members on the other side than is usually the case, I have no hope of this bill going beyond this today. However, 1 urge with all the strength I can that members on the government side take steps to emphasize to the members of the cabinet, the Prime

Minister, and the Attorney General (Mr. Basford) that the public is ready for a reform of this kind.
I am perfectly satisfied that, far from increasing the number of divorces, legislation of this kind will probably lessen them. Using the grounds under the present law, manufactured evidence, and I am sure it exists now as it did 15 or 20 years ago when I knew what was going on, is probably used to obtain divorces without any attempt to provide for a reconciliation. A proper application of the philosophy contained in this bill would go a long distance toward minimizing the number of divorces. It would make certain that when the condition of the marriage had reached the stage where it was quite plain that nothing on God's green earth could save it, it would be dissolved. That is the kind of law we need.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have some notes I would like to go through. Before I start, however, there are a couple of things which were said by previous speakers with which I would like to take issue.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) alluded to the fact that under the present system the judges of our courts have no right, obligation or, in his view, desire to satisfy themselves that there is no possibility of reconciliation in these cases. If the hon. member had practised under the new law, which apparently he has not, he would have had the opportunity to know that before any court in this land can deal with divorce at this time, the first obligation of the judge, before the witnesses are even sworn, is to satisfy himself that there is no possibility of reconciliation.
In all cases and in all the courts in which I have appeared on matrimonial matters, I have never seen a judge fail to discharge that obligation. It might have been cursory. It might have been insufficient in terms of what the hon. member would like to see happen. However, it is required by the present act and, in my experience, it is done.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Holt) brought a very pessimistic approach to this House. I would like to add a little positivism from my point of view and experience, having done a substantial amount of family law work before coming to this honourable place.
The hon. member indicated that in no instance had she found that reconciliation ever took place once a marriage was on the rocks, or words to that effect. I would like to suggest to this House that on at least three occasions I have had the courts interject in the middle of the divorce proceedings and challenge both parties in the divorce cases that in fact reconciliation had not been tried enough. I had three that were sent back by judges. In fact reconciliation did take place and they are still together. It may not work as much as we would like, but it is working in some instances. It is not as pessimistic as the hon. member believes.
Like the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), I agree there is a need for change in the divorce law. Having dealt with it, I am satisfied there is room for change. In the area of family law, reform should be introduced only after very careful study. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) expressed this

point of view very well in his speech to the Family Law Section, Ontario Bar Association, in Toronto on January 26. I will not repeat his words. I ask only that hon. members interested in this particular issue look at the text of his speech at that time.
In speaking of the process of reform in which the government is now engaged, I shall assume, Mr. Speaker, that most hon. members are aware of the general nature of the recommendations of the Law Reform Commission of Canada, some of which the hon. member for Greenwood is asking us to enact in his bill. I should therefore like to direct my remarks more to the process of government consultation and the conscious effort to find a national consensus in the field of family law. I am directing my attention to these matters in order to explain why I think that it would be premature at this time to enact the bill proposed by the hon. member.
Following close upon receipt by the Minister of Justice of the Report of the Law Reform Commission on Family Law, the attorneys general met in Vancouver in June to discuss, among other things, family law and the administration of that law in the courts. The ministers agreed that it was important to move quickly to establish unified family courts, and there was a general recognition that both levels of government must move forward toward adopting the concept of marriage as a partnership of equals. During their conference the provincial ministers expressed the view that matrimonial property is exclusively a provincial matter. They agreed to urge their governments to press forward with matrimonial property law reform. There was a feeling that matrimonial property law reform should precede divorce reform.
The view that matrimonial property law reform should precede or accompany divorce reform is a view shared by a number of women's groups. They are worried that, if the grounds for divorce are changed before the matrimonial property laws are changed, then a wife who is economically dependent upon her husband could be deprived of her bargaining power in the dissolution process. 1 would not want to imply that these women's groups do not want a divorce reform. They are clearly dissatisfied with the divorce law as it now stands, but consider that any reform that would require a woman to support herself after a reasonable period of time must be accompanied by a property division that would reflect her participation in and contribution to the marriage.
By these arguments the federal government should wait and delay its reform of the Divorce Act until the law on matrimonial property is changed. On the other hand, as the Law Reform Commission emphasized, present divorce procedures are unsatisfactory because they are counter productive, that is, they aggravate problems rather than help to solve them. This happens, as the commission suggests, because the Divorce Act embodies the concept of marital offence or faults. To change the ground for divorce from fault to permanent breakdown or irretrievable breakdown, as suggested in the bill proposed by the hon. member, would be to move away from
March 1, 1977

the adversary approach to divorce and to introduce a greater possibility of conciliatory action. This, perhaps, is an ideal, but if I could get away from my notes for a moment 1 would suggest to the House that I myself had an unfortunate experience with regard to the way in which the new legislation works out in practice. Where there is deemed to be a breakdown of marriage after so many years of separation, trained social workers are supposed to determine whether or not there has in fact been an irreconcilable family breakdown. I found that many of these trained persons relied on form-type letters to be checked off and signed by the individuals involved, and that they frequently advised the court that there had been a breakdown of a marriage without even having seen the parties involved.

speechtext: Shame!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO STIPULATE "BREAKDOWN PRINCIPLE" SOLE BASIS FOR DIVORCE
speechtext:
I think that is a crying shame, as the hon. member for Greenwood said. Unfortunately the legislation now proposed could lead to even greater abuses unless we protect ourselves.
The Minister of Justice is well aware of both sides of the issue: the need, on the one hand, for property law reform to precede or coincide with divorce reform and for new courts or court services to be in place in order to permit new divorce procedures to be introduced; and the importance, on the other hand, of pressing forward with the actual divorce reform itself. That is why he said in his speech to the Family Law Section of the Ontario Bar Association to which 1 earlier referred, and I quote,
I would point out to the remaining provinces, however, and indeed to the legislatures of Ontario and British Columbia (as distinct from the government's of those two provinces), that if, as they say, matrimonial property is a matter within their exclusive jurisdiction, then they have a responsibility to act and to act expeditiously. If the provinces do not move expeditiously to put in place meaningful changes in the law relating to matrimonial property to take account of the economic needs and the rights of both spouses, there will obviously be increasing pressure on the federal parliament to endeavour to try to implement the recommendations, in one form or another, of the Law Reform Commission's report relating to the disposal of matrimonial property. Canadian women should not have to wait much longer for provincial action in this regard.
Before proceeding to discuss the details of the bill proposed by the hon. member, 1 should like to say a few more words in respect of another matter that I have already touched on- family courts. One of the reasons for proceeding slowly in divorce reform is the need to put into place new unified family courts or family court services in existing courts. If there is to be a movement away from the adversary system toward a more conciliatory approach to divorce, then counselling services in the courts are necessary. Other services such as investigatory services and enforcement services would be useful. If there is to be an automatic enforcement of maintenance orders, then enforcement services will be vital. The development of these courts takes time and is costly.
The federal government is encouraging the provinces in their efforts to create these courts by providing money to enable the joint funding of experimental unified family court pilot projects of various types to test a number of possible alternatives. Discussions in respect of such projects are under
Divorce
way at the present time with the provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Newfoundland. Further, the government is sharing in the funding of the evaluation of the unified family court pilot project that was undertaken by the province of British Columbia in 1974. It is hoped that from these experiments valuable guidelines will be drawn for the future development of family courts in Canada.
I am sure many hon. members will be aware of the announcement made on February 17 last with respect to the appointment of judges to the first unified family court in the Hamilton-Wentworth area. Some of these problems are highlighted by the fact that, following this announcement, a number of people opposed the appointments saying they had come too quickly, that it would be a disaster, that the family court as presently established could never handle the overwhelming weight of this type of action particularly when this involved property and its disposition.
Speaking directly to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Greenwood, I should like to say that while I think it is premature to attempt to replace the Divorce Act at this time and in this way, I agree with some of the principles upon which the bill is based.

speechtext: Question!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO STIPULATE "BREAKDOWN PRINCIPLE" SOLE BASIS FOR DIVORCE
speechtext:
The bill is inadequate in that it would repeal the Divorce Act but not replace many of the provisions of the Divorce Act that are essential to a scheme of divorce. For example, the bill does not deal with the subject of how the maintenance and custody orders made by a court in one province would be enforced in another province. This is an important problem that must be dealt with in any new divorce act.
Taking the clauses in their order, I would first have to comment that the definition "court" is not adequate. First, it does not reflect the correct names and divisions of the Superior Courts that hear divorces in various provinces. I think the hon. member is probably not aware of the amendments to the Divorce Act that changed these definitions. Also, I do not think that it is necessary to make reference to the county or district courts of the province. In a number of provinces, judges of the county and district courts hear divorces but, in such cases, they do so as local judges of the Superior Court of the province. When acting as local judges of the Superior Court, they have jurisdiction to hear property matters that they would not have jurisdiction to hear if they were sitting as judges of the county or district courts. While, in the future, it may become possible for divorces to be heard in courts other than Superior Courts, at the moment, for constitutional reasons, it would seem better to retain the jurisdiction in the superior courts and provide that cases may be heard by judges of those courts or local judges thereof. Clause 3 gives me some problems also. While I have some sympathy with the idea of granting divorces on the basis of irretrievable or permanent marriage breakdown. I question how the courts would view the words in subclause 3(2). If it were to be necessary to prove that there is "no reasonable possibility of reconciliation", trials

March 1, 1977
National Transportation Act
to determine this question would probably continue to be necessary and many divorces that it would be reasonable to grant might be refused.
Subclause 3(3) relieves the onus of proof to a considerable extent by providing that where the parties have lived separate and apart for a year the marriage shall be deemed to be irretrievably broken down. However, nothing in the bill prohibits the parties from commencing an action prior to that year of separation. In those cases, acrimonious trials would probably continue. Spouses would still be coming to the court to make allegations against each other. I think that the hon. member wishes to provide for no-fault divorce and would not, himself, wish to see this new type of trial develop as a result of his bill. In order to avoid this result, it would probably be necessary either to prohibit divorces to be heard before the expiration of a year of separation, or to provide for proof that the marriage has irretrievably broken down to be given by some kind of non-accusatory evidence. I should like to see any bill put forward on the subject of divorce contain some provisions that would reduce the adversary aspects of the divorce proceeding and promote reconciliation and the preservation of the family unit to the extent possible.
The promotion of reconciliation brings me to another problem I find in the bill. I am not convinced it should be necessary for parties to live separate and apart for a year in order to qualify for a divorce. I think this is one of the problems with the present Divorce Act. The requirement for separation inhibits the possibility of reconciliation.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate adjourned at five o'clock I was talking about the illogical efforts of the government, with the support of the official opposition, to retain competition and commercial viability in transportation. I said that if it were logical to have competing railroads and competing air lines, it would be just as logical to have competing sewage and water systems, streets, highways, telephone lines, and power lines. I want to quote a further excerpt from the speech made by the former leader of our party, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), in the debate similar to this one which we had in 1966. On that occasion he said:
The fact is that I do not believe that free enterprise and the competitive system of transportation can give Canada an adequate transportation policy at a price we can afford ... in a country of 20 million people, where ... we are more dependent than probably any country in the world on getting our goods to market over long distances at competitive prices, where we spend more per capita on transportation than probably any other country in the world, I do not think we can afford the luxury of having a free enterprise, competitive transportation policy ... I believe that what we need is more government control and direction, not less, in the field of transportation.
Those words are as valid today as they were in 1966. Competition between modes of transportation mis-allocates resources, in fact, wastes resources, through the inappropriate use of each mode. When it comes to rates, if a railway rate is too high, why not have the government intervene to regulate the rate? The free enterprise competitive system says that instead you should foster intermodal competition to hold the rate down by building another super highway parallel to a railway line, or subsidizing another railway line, or subsidizing some more airports and air lines.
I hope we will agree that it would be foolish, for example, to promote the trucking of heavy bulk commodities, such as coal, potash, fertilizer, iron ore or grain, over medium and long distances. Not only is it foolish, it is too costly in terms of energy and in terms of the misuse of a particular mode of transportation, namely, trucking. Truck transport of bulk commodities requires four to six times as much energy as rail transport.
Competition between modes of transportation denies the stated objective in the bill of integrating the modes together. For example, a bus company is not going to short haul itself to serve as a feeder to railway lines if it can get a full haul for its own revenues. Instead of intermodal competition, why not intermodal co-ordination? Why not integrate passenger ticket offices, baggage handling facilities and passenger terminals in common facilities? In many cases the facility already exists in former downtown railway stations.
Let me give an illustration, Mr. Speaker. In my own city of Regina, Air Canada established a new downtown ticket office in the new Toronto-Dominion Bank building which is very posh and plush. There are exactly two spaces to park a car in front of that building, and they are in a two-minute zone. If you want to buy an airline ticket, you will have to drive and then park your car several blocks away, if you can find a
March 1, 1977

parking place. This may give a good image for Air Canada's brass, but it is hardly the place to encourage people to come in and buy their airline ticket.
There is a downtown railway station in Regina with ample parking facilities which are mostly unused. This is where the Air Canada ticket office should be, and where the CN and CP railway ticket offices should be. This is where the terminal for the airport limousine should be, where the taxi stand should be, where the city transit busses should stop, and where the bus ticket offices should be. Instead of that, we have the so called intermodal competition. They all have separate buildings and separate ticket offices, all of which adds to the cost of transportation in our country.
That kind of commercial viability and competition in transportation is sheer economic nonsense. No self-respecting free enterpriser or businessman, in that kind of enterprise or any other kind, would willingly or knowingly resort to such an operation. But as long as you have old line party governments which cling to nineteenth century mythology about competition and commercial viability in transportation, you will have those kinds of boondoggles in every city in this country.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
As I said before five o'clock, the elimination of competition and commercial viability in transportation is not some socialist dogma. It is not just some ideology of the NDP. It is a fact in countries all over the world with governments of all political persuasion, from the extreme left to the extreme right and everything in between. Canada, and to a lesser degree the United States, remain the only two still clinging to this mythology of competition in transportation. The days of the railroad barons and "maggots" of the 1880's and 1890's are gone.
Commercial viability for a transportation company may deny the economic needs of an individual community or of our nation as a whole. We submit that service to the public and national and regional economic objectives should take precedence over profitability. For example, in freight rates the maximum rate provisions in this legislation are virtually worthless since the maximum ceiling is so high that railway companies may charge whatever they deem suitable.
Let me illustrate with some specific examples where people are discriminated against because of where they happen to live. The agreed charge rate for food stuffs-and I wish the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn) were here because the agreed charge rate for food stuffs applies also to Saskatoon-hauled from Toronto to Vancouver is 2.63 cents a ton mile, but it is 3.53 cents a ton mile from Toronto to Saskatoon. An average of seven different agreed charges indicates that the railways are charging 53.4 per cent more per ton mile for like goods hauled from Toronto to Saskatoon than from Toronto to Vancouver.

The other items on freight rates that I want to comment on now are, for example, the prairie rapeseed crushing industry. They face inequities because it is more economical to ship raw rapeseed to central Canada for crushing instead of processing it on the prairies and shipping the processed products. Under the new rates-and I hope the hon. member for Assiniboia will make a speech and tell us how this will be corrected-published by the Canadian Transport Commission for rapeseed products, it costs 62.4 cents more per hundredweight to ship rapeseed products than it does to ship raw rapeseed from Saskatoon to Montreal. The previous dif-

ference was 25.3 cents; now it is 62.4 cents. The answer of the Minister of Transport to this inequity would be to jack up the rate on raw rapeseed so that it would move at a compensatory rate. This would price the western rapeseed products right out of the central Canadian market. They would no longer be competing with corn, peanuts, soyabeans, coconut oil or sunflower oil. It prices western processed rapeseed oil right out of the central Canadian market, let alone the export market.
It is bad enough when this happens under the Liberal Minister of Transport, but this had a lot of help from the Conservatives. They sold out to the government, as usual. I listened very carefully to the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner), who did not take any position on the bill one way or another except horizontal. He is neither for or against the bill. This is typical. It is no longer Joe who or Joe what, it is Jack what. On this issue of the processing of rapeseed in western Canada, the minister of transport in Alberta, who happens to be a relative of the hon. member for Crowfoot, not only opposed extending the statutory rate to rapeseed products but suggested that raw rapeseed be taken off the statutory grain rate. That is a lot of help from those Conservatives in Alberta.
The Tories talk motherhood about promoting decentralization and regional industry, but where are they when it comes down to the nitty-gritty of the future of our rapeseed industry in western Canada? They fell into line with profitability and commercial viability and said, "Take rapeseed off the Crows-nest pass rates". Like the Atlantic premiers, the premier of Alberta sold out. The Tories agreed with the Minister of Transport that there has to be competition and that there has to be commercial viability in transportation. The official opposition did nothing but some nitpicking with regard to this legislation. 1 listened to the hon. member for Crowfoot, and I like the man very much, but he did not take a stand.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before beginning my speech, may I say that I disagree with the government leader for having introduced this bill today, not because I am against the introduction of a bill on transportation, but because we were informed only half an hour before the House resumed of the change in the business of the House. Today we were supposed to discuss Bill C-27 on unemployment insurance and we got ready for that. A few minutes only before entering the House, we were told that the government had changed its mind and that we would be discussing Bill C-33 on transportation.
I asked why this sudden change. The answer was that this was because the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) was in the House and he wanted to introduce his bill himself, but here we were in for another surprise: the presentation was made by the Minister of Justice on behalf of the Minister of Transport. This demonstrates again the lack of planning on the part of the government in submitting the other leaders in the House an orderly schedule. We are lost in conjectures about the real reasons behind these changes which were made at the very last minute.
Still I am pleased to see this bill introduced because I have a lot to say about the administration of the Canadian National and about the passenger service which these officials seem to discredit. I see some of them up there smiling and conferring. They know they are protected because they sit behind the minister; it is impossible to find the name of a single one or to know their opinion about the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area.
For the last 15 years I have been struggling in this House to save to some extent what is left of the passenger service in our area. Barely 15 years after the flourishing period of our railway, we were visited by so-called specialists from the large cities; they closed all the passenger stations; they turned express and postal services over to the private sector because it gave them too much work; they dismissed all employees in those services and suppressed two thirds of the personnel entrusted with the maintenance of the railroad track and tripled the clerical work force. They forgot one thing: trains best operate on well-maintained railroad tracks and not on television screens. Even though the contrary may seem true, it was wishful thinking on their part. Today we have a bill dealing with railways and whose first clause reads as follows:
.. . the National Transportation Act is repealed . . .
We spend our time in the House repealing laws to replace them by others which are sometimes less efficient-
"3. (1) It is hereby declared that the objective of the transportation policy for Canada is to achieve a transportation system that
(a)	is efficient,
(b)	is an effective instrument of support for the achievement of national and
regional social and economic objectives, and
(r) provides accessibility and equity of treatment for users,.. .

All that makes me laugh, Mr. Speaker. And we read in the recommendation that it is for the purpose of defining the objective of the transportation policy for Canada and authorizing the consequential rearrangement of powers. The rearrangement of powers and duties relating to transport, now that is important!
Mr. Speaker, when talking about rearrangement of powers and relations in transport, it means another change in the staff. As you see, there will be another rearrangement of responsibilities in the field of transport. In short, what do these proposals mean? More technocrats and bureaucrats who are going to strut about like their predecessors or spend their time sleeping in their sumptuously furnished offices.
We may read the whole bill but at the end at the very last line, Mr. Speaker, we read that the Minister of Transport will decide. What does that mean? It means that technocrats will keep their own preserve in the field of Canadian transport. That is that! Technocrats are never mentioned, they only refer to the minister, but we know very well what it means.
That was a realistic summary of Bill C-33. Mr. Speaker, it would be better for us to keep only the last line of the bill and throw the balance into the wastebasket, because in the end decisions will not be made in the House, but elsewhere. The goal of the bill is to meet the regional needs in an efficient fashion. If I had time to read again the bills on transportation passed since Confederation, I would always find the same goals set out, perhaps with a different terminology. That is a good indication how our high officials repeat themselves.
Then the minister tells us that the bill is aimed at combining the various means of transportation and set up joint public and private services. It has been done for a long time, Mr. Speaker. And I would add that if our public carrier did not have its annual deficits paid by the taxpayers, I mean freight transport, never could it compete with the private sector. As far as freight transportation is concerned, our public carrier was anxious to hide its own administrative incompetence, hence the agreements with its competitor, that is private enterprise.
I wish I had more time to provide you with background information on these freight rates. I should have a lot to say but I prefer to make use of my own time telling you about passenger services generally-since this bill deals also with this-but more specifically in my own Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean region. Someone may say that this is not the first time I have raised this issue in the House. However, following the remarks I made in the House the other day, I feel this is an excellent opportunity to tell you about this famous train.
I am afraid someone has called down curses from heaven upon our region, for technocrats have apparently decided to put down or even make us hate the only passenger service which has survived the devastating attacks launched by Montreal officials. Especially in the past 15 years officials have been anxious to prove to the authorities of the country that a railway in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area is not profitable. Every trick has been used, such as no adequate maintenance of
National Transportation Act
the tracks and antiquated passenger cars. They have even used the suburban cars of Montreal to provide service between Montreal-Chicoutimi-Dolbeau or still

speechtext: Jonquiere.

speechtext:
-Jonquiere is also included, so that the tracks are left clear for freight trains while passengers have to wait for hours and hours on a siding because freight trains have priority. We have to say how we are treated in our area. Or the passenger from the Dolbeau-Chicoutimi train must cool his heels for two or three hours at Hervey-Jonction waiting for a train from Abitibi when it would be more logical to proceed directly to Montreal as it has been done each Sunday night for years. But during the week one has to wait for the Abitibi train which must travel to Montreal in two and a half or three hours. As the Abitibi train is always late, we arrive late in Montreal. That's it! Finally, the favorite sport of senior civil servants is to play with schedules. They are interested in schedules, they often play with them. They juggle with them. It is a little like the torment of the drop of water. The latest draft schedule for April 1977 has not been published yet, but I have it. It is concrete evidence of what I just said.
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, that according to that new schedule, any passenger from Chicoutimi, Jonquiere, Chambord or Dol-beau will leave Chicoutimi at one p.m. From Dolbeau, he will leave at noon and arrive in Montreal around 11.30 p.m. We might as well say midnight, because there is always a halfhour delay.
When I saw this schedule, I thought it was the height of stupidity. Those people should either go and see a psychiatrist or be confined. They are due for some mental rest. Let's imagine someone going to Montreal on business. Right now he can leave Dolbeau or Chicoutimi at seven in the evening. At 6:30 in the morning he gets into Montreal, does his business, and then at eight or nine o'clock in the evening he is ready to take the train back home. He does not lose time. Two nights aboard a sleeping car or a coach during eight and a half or nine hours. But with the new schedule, the train will leave Chicoutimi at noon and arrive at midnight: so the businessman getting into Montreal at night will have to check in a hotel, spend the night in Montreal and do his business the following day; but since the train leaves for Chicoutimi at seven in the morning, he will have to wait for the next morning train to go back to Chicoutimi. So he will have to take two days and three nights for his business. Anyone can imagine what results this schedule will have. And now, Mr. Speaker, this schedule will become effective on April 1.
Starting April 1, this schedule will be implemented. Never, and I want parliament to note this, never before would any public servants have had the gall to suggest such a ridiculous schedule. We can now imagine what the situation will be for the hundreds of workers who leave each fall for the fruit and vegetable harvest in Ontario, for the 600 to 800 workers, for entire families, who take the train to Ontario. They will reach

March 1, 1977
National Transportation Act
Montreal at midnight and they will have to spend the night on the floor of the station waiting for the train next day. With the present schedule, they reach Montreal at 6 or 6:30, which means that they can transfer as soon as they get off the train to another train going to Ontario. This is why, on February 28, I presented a motion in the House to appeal to the Minister of Transport so that this decision may be postponed for six months. My motion, dated February 28, reads as follows:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion dealing with a matter of utmost importance and urgency to the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area.
As according to the new CN passenger service schedule becoming effective in early April, the only passenger train will be arriving into Montreal at 23:30, as at that late hour all connection with other trains is impossible and as, according to that new schedule, three days and two nights will be needed to spend one business day in Montreal, that waste of time never having existed previously because the same trip is now made during the night, and as the implementation of that new schedule will cause serious prejudice to the travelling public in the area to the extent where the clientele will disappear, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Allard):
That the Minister of Transport exert immediately the required pressure
with the CN president and Mr. Jean-Marie Beaulieu-
-He seems to be in charge there-
-general superintendent, to delay the implementation of the new schedule for six months, with a view to allowing local organizations to present their suggestions in that regard.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if this time the minister will have the courage to act in the interest of the public, because 1 suspect premeditation on the part of the public servants who thought up this schedule change to try to prove to the minister that the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean passenger train was no longer necessary because of a lack of customers. We can expect anything these days, especially on the part of those who have nothing to think about in their office except how to do a disservice to others while pretending that they are helping them. With such a schedule, who will want to take the train to spend two nights in a hotel in Montreal? Once again, if the minister wants to meet his objectives and meet the needs of the travelling public, he will have to eliminate certain public servants who are dedicated to destroying everything. One thing encourages me however, and this is the news reported in the newspaper Le Devoir of March 1, 1977, and I quote:
Lang Annouces Creation of VIA Rail for Passengers Federal Transport Minister Otto Lang announced yesterday the creation of VIA Rail Canada to operate passenger train services.
In announcing the news, Mr. Lang said the new corporation will be a subsidiary of Canadian National Railways, with plans and budgets subject to government approval.
Creation of the new corporation comes three years after it was first mentioned by the government in the 1974 election campaign.
That is where I started wondering, is he preparing another election campaign?
VIA Rail will take over routes gradually from CN and CP Rail, starting with that part of the network located in the Quebec-Windsor axis. Other lines will follow later.
I hope ours would be turned over immediately.
The Minister of Transport said the government is ready to contribute to capital requirements for trains and track and help with operating losses. Nevertheless, the government is now considering with CN and CP Rail ways to improve performance and minimize costs.

The new company will contract with CN and CP for the operation of passenger trains on existing routes.
The name of VIA Rail president will be known later this week. Already, Frank Roberts, now vice-president of CN's St. Lawrence region, is understood to be the choice.
That is precisely our area. I had heard that Mr. Roberts would be the president of the new corporation. I am very pleased with that, and I ask him to correct the mistakes of his predecessors and give our area a little bit more justice. I am convinced that if a good passenger service is set up between Montreal-Chambord via Dolbeau-Chicoutimi since the run goes well from Chambord to Montreal between 8 and 8:30, at night-I repeat at night-because of the energy restrictions that will soon be mandatory people will be surprised to see how well it will stand up against the competition, even of buses and airlines, because it is proved that rail service is always more reliable. I therefore ask the new president to hold an inquiry in the area and invite all hon. members, who will make it their duty to accept his invitation, to discuss that famous problem of passengers and solve it once and for all.
The problem will never be solved by civil servants in Montreal who barely know the area having gone there only a few times and, mind you, by plane. Mr. Speaker, I promise to ask all companies in the area to use the freight trains, and appeal to all municipal councils, all Chambers of Commerce and local R.D.C.s to prove to the minister and the CN that a passenger service is needed in my area; if it is improved, through both services and schedules, the clientele will triple within a year. Of course, the image of that mode of transport will have to be uplifted because it has been rather battered in the last few years.
Meanwhile, we must keep the current schedule before taking further decisions following the consultations I have suggested earlier. Indeed these consultations could deal with ticket prices, rates for beds-the actual rate is a ridiculous $45-and finally with everything that could attract the clientele and guarantee a satisfactory passenger service. One must never forget that the passenger train is first of all a customer service. It is not a money making industry but government officials are trying to convince the population that it must be a paying proposition. It is not worse than in other regions. The same goes for all other public services whose purpose is to offer the public a better service. Besides, the Canadian Transport Commission has come to the same conclusion and 1 quote Le Devoir of March 1, 1977:
The Canadian Transport Commission has already come to the conclusion that there is not a single profit making trunk line in all of Canada .. .
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that we are no worse off than these regions. No better, but no worse! We want the same services as the other regions.

we discuss this important bill, C-33, effectively. It concerns rail passenger policy. It concerns not only national transportation policy but amends the Railway Act. It has an effect on the Canadian Transport Commission.
Transportation is an extremely difficult and complicated business for most Canadians. Canadians in the urban centres can never understand why members of parliament spend so much time on matters of transportation. Naturally, they use such things as urban transit, streetcars and buses and they do not understand the special difficulties in the west with regard to moving grain.
Members opposite are making remarks at the moment because they do not have the courtesy to listen to a few of my remarks, although I spent a lot of time listening to theirs. The hon. member who spoke previously spoke for 40 minutes on a rather contradictory speech. We sat here and listened to him. 1 should think he would let me get on with my few remarks.
Many of the people I represent understand the fact that transportation is one of the things that brought Canada together in the first place. The railway is a part of Canadian history. They know the story of the CPR and the way that railway had to be built in order to bring this country together. Perhaps it is appropriate that this subject be raised again at this time.
There are members in the House of Commons who represent areas in the maritimes which are concerned about better air service. We know of the difficulties in British Columbia with the coastal ferry service. There are many difficulties in Toronto with urban transit, such as the tremendous costs for subway construction and buying the kinds of vehicles needed to run a modern city. Even a few years ago this would not have been considered for the national government. It was a provincial and municipal problem. Now it has become so costly that the amounts of money required can only be provided by a national government.
I can only speak of the Toronto area with some knowledge. We have always understood that transportation in Canada has never been a paying proposition. We have always had to cough up. We have had to pay a lot of money because in this country we do not have the concentrations of population which makes transportation an easy matter to deal with.
We have the problems of freight subsidies, ferry subsidies, rail passenger subsidies, and other subsidies as well. I was looking at some of the figures. In his speech this afternoon the minister pointed out the deficit. Deficits can always be argued because the figures are so hard to obtain. But according to the minister's statement this afternoon, the deficit was $1.6 billion in 1975-76 to operate the Ministry of Transport in all the areas of Canada with which the Ministry of Transport deals.
Now, philosophically, I agree with some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). Transportation in Canada is crucial to the unity of this country. I hesitate to use that word which is being thrown around these days. But it is the concern of all of us.
National Transportation Act
The fact is that transportation is as important in Canada today as it was in 1867. In fact it may be more important. In 1957-58 the whole world started travelling at 550 miles an hour, the speed of a jet plane. As the former minister of manpower and immigration knows, there have been scenes in this House with regard to immigration matters because populations can move around this planet at 550 miles an hour. That is something that has never been seen before and it has to be dealt with in this age.
But originally it was the railway that.brought us together physically. Now we have the problem of what form of transportation should be used to bring us together. That is the big question which this House spends so much time discussing.
I have some figures. The cost of operating a railway is phenomenal. I am not using this as an argument not to subsidize the railways, but while the number of passengers declined 1 per cent between 1972 and 1974, the deficit rose 30 per cent. That is the kind of problem with which we have to deal. How do we go about what is needed to run our railway efficiently when the costs are so tremendous?
I was born and raised in Canada. Yet I could not afford to visit the city of Vancouver before being elected to the House of Commons. I imagine that was the case for many members of the House. I think most members get the picture.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre referred to Europe in his speech. We have this habit of talking about how well the railway system operates in Europe and how poorly it operates here. In Europe there are high population concentrations that are fairly close together. They are easily served.
In the 1950's the government of France made a conscious decision to put its investments in the railways. When the French delegation left Paris for the Rome talks in 1958, they took the train. The delegation did not meet at the airport the way we do here. They met at the Gare de Lyons. It is a 15 hours trip to Rome. It is a good trip. The other side of the coin is that you cannot rely on airline service to get you from Paris to Rome. Those of us who have had the experience of European airlines know that their standards are not up to Canadian standards.
We talk about the tremendous railway system they have across the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union must have the best rail line I have ever seen in my life. It is fantastic the way it runs between the Soviet Far East and Europe. They do a tremendous business in trans-shipping. The railway line is several tracks wide for thousands of miles and it is most efficient. Any Canadian who rides it cannot believe that this is what a railway can be like. Of course, if he looks outside the train he notices there are no roads. They do not have any roads, and most Canadians probably feel they would like to have roads as well as a railway, and also they would like to have airplanes as well as a railway.
In Canada effectively we have a choice. We want all of them. We want everything. We want the ferries, we want the roads, we want the airlines, and we want the trains. I think

that in Canada we should have the trains. We have a society with enough experience to find a proper balance between these various modes of transportation.
Something which has become apparent to me over the past few years since I have been here as a member of parliament is that we have given too much power to the Canadian Transport Commission.

The Conservative transportation critic who spoke earlier today gave me the impression that he did not think politicians should make political decisions about transportation in Canada. 1 think that is crazy. We are not talking about just a few thousands of dollars. To my way of thinking, $1.6 billion is a lot of money, it is a heck of a lot of money. Allocating large sums between various forms of transportation has been a national question for more than a hundred years, so when an hon. member suggests to me there should not be political input into the question of how this money should be spent, I just think that is crazy.
Over the last few months we have had experience with Polysar. We have had our experiences with these different agencies which were set up in the 1940's and the 1950's. This is not a problem which is unique to Canada. This is common in many countries. There are only 265 of us. We have to do all the things which have to be done. There are committees, and all members know how busy they are. I guess at some point we decided we ought to establish an independent commission to do this, an independent committee to do that, and a non-political thingamajig to do this, and another mechanism here to do that. And the first thing we know, we have the Minister of Transport standing up in the House of Commons saying "It's a mess, it's awful, and I cannot do anything about it because 1 don't have the political control necessary to resolve this very difficult question."
We are dealing with a very complex issue, but I think that when I see on the first or the second page of Bill C-33 that we are redefining the objective of the transportation policy for Canada, and when I see this business that we are amending the functions, powers and duties of the Canadian Transport Commission, nothing gives me greater joy. A step is finally being taken to get the kind of control back over the transportation system in this country that the government should have.
Members opposite are talking about Pickersgill in 1966 or 1967. Well, it is 1977 now. They may have forgotten it, but we are living in 1977, so we are prepared to acknowledge that reforms have to be made because we have gone a little bit forward, we have found things that are not right and we are
