speechtext:
It just might be that I will support this aberration because, God knows, anything is better than nothing. We have had nothing for ten years. Perhaps it is a step in the right direction, but there are things we want to know about. What is it going to do for the port of Halifax? What is it going to do for the "at and east" rates? Where is all this grand money about which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) tells our Atlantic premiers? All these words mean nothing.
The degree to which this piece of legislation will be affected and will be well received politically by the people in Atlantic Canada will be measured by the degree to which the minister does something with regard to the powers he will give to himself. Before giving him those powers, I want to know what he is talking about. I want to know where the extra funds will come from. I want to know what he is talking about when he says we will not only get rid of ineffective and inefficient subsidy programs, not only will we take that money and give it to the economically depressed regions to upgrade their transportation facilities, but we will find more money. Where is that money coming from and what will he do with it?
He went to the Atlantic provinces and came out of there with the blush of sunshine, praised by everybody about his user-pay principle reversal. How will he forgo that? It shows up here in the bill. The concept is there about avoiding it where economic contingencies come to the fore, and it should be avoided or set to one side. It has been there for a long time. What he is going to do for us, what is he going to do for Canada? All that he is doing here is to take unto himself enormous powers.
Let us go through the principles for a minute or two, the eight or ten principles. It says: the federal government will establish the national policies and the CTC will enforce them. How have we been running transport for the last 30 or 40 years if it has not been that way?
It says that the development and regulation of the transport system will be done in co-operation with all levels of government and the public. Probably I will support this bill on second reading, but before I do I want to hear from the minister-not the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) but the Minister of Transport-and from some members from Atlantic Canada.
[Mr. Forrestali.)
How will they consult with the general public about something as broad and sweeping as that particular principle? I welcome it, it has to be done, but stand up and tell me how you intend to do it.
It says here that competition within and between transport modes will be encouraged where other considerations permit. What other considerations? What are you talking about? What does that mean? Do not ask us to buy something unless you are prepared to tell us what it means and what it is all about.
It says here that conflict between public and private interests will be resolved in favour of the public interests. I am down to paragraph (d). I think Sir John A. Macdonald talked about this 110 years ago. What else is there? A little bit of mother love so far.
It says here that there should be opportunities for both public and private ownership, national, regional, and local carriers, and for Canadian ownership of private carriers. What does that last little tagged-on phrase mean? You have all spoken to your truckers, to people in the transportation industry, and you know exactly what it means. There is enough authority in that one sentence to make a dictator out of the minister if he wants to be one. Why? We will not give it to him until we have heard. That is the purpose of our being here.
It says here that commercial viability for both transportation and related services is an objective. Of course it is a desired and good objective, but stand up and tell me what it means.
It says here: where government policy militates against commercial viability, the benefits and costs involved should be identified and the additional costs assumed by the government. What will that apply to? Will it help our neighbours, the provincial people in Prince Edward Island to move their potatoes to the mainland, or to move other produce into Newfoundland or out to the Madgalen Islands? Is that what it means, and if so how will it happen, because these are the things that are important?
It says here: the market place will determine costs and services where effective competition exists; where it does not, these will be regulated to give users the same protection that the competition will give them. It is not the market place that will protect them. The minister has assumed that right and responsibility himself. He has the power and the authority. When he stands up and tells me what he is going to do, only then will we make a decision on whether or not this is a useful and meaningful step in the right direction. Until he does, let him sit there and think about an area of Canada that cannot survive without an efficient and competitive transportation system.
We do not have a market area of 600,000 people to support secondary manufacturing in industry other than in the primary products such as forestry, fishing, and our coal industry. We cannot make shirts. We do not have enough people to sell them to within reasonable transportation distance. We have to come back up to Montreal or Toronto to get rid of our surplus

production just to maintain the efficiency of our plants, and our plants are not inefficient due to bad management but they are hamstrung by ad hocery. There is nothing wrong with the word ad hoc. It is a good, useful word. Perhaps if it had been employed ten years ago, bit by bit we might have had some semblance of a transportation policy. I say it is ad hoc because it deals with a section of transportation. It refers to air, it refers to water, it refers to the upgrading and improving of the road system. It refers to taking dollars from this system and giving them to another system. Do not tell us all that vaguely without telling us what you are going to do.
One could go on with that for the next hour. There has to be the widest possible input in our discussion with respect to this because, while it sounds good and encouraging to those of us who live in areas totally dependent on transportation, I suggest that it skates awfully close to a very dangerous precipice.
What does the minister mean when he says to us that he is going to do away with subsidies that are inefficient and ineffective? Will he use those subsidies to give more appropriate help to some of the regions of Canada to overcome the disparity?
In the bulletin of the Ministry of Transport of February 8, Bulletin No. 18, at page 3 we are told about the agreements arrived at between the Minister of Transport and the Council of Maritime premiers meeting together with Mr. Morgan of Newfoundland. It reads:
Mr. Lang, Mr. Morgan and the Maritime premiers agreed in principle that improved passenger transportation could best be achieved by providing special assistance for upgrading bus and air services in that region, to be followed by changes to existing rail passenger-services, for which the demand is relatively low-
In the name of all that is holy how can we improve rail transportation by improving air services and bus services? Perhaps we can. We can in Newfoundland because the Bullet has been closed down. All there is from Port aux Basques to St. John's is a bus, and no doubt my friends and colleagues from Newfoundland can wax eloquently about that and about the difficulty that has been caused in that province with respect to its provincial transportation system.
However, leaving that little bit of logic to one side because, after all, this is just a press report, and it obviously was not written by politicians who have the answers to everything-or should have, according to some speakers here this evening- what does the minister mean when he says passenger services can be improved by operating air services and road services? Are we going to get dollars and cents to bring our highways up to Trans-Canada standards so that we can move potatoes from one end of Prince Edward Island to a dockside, so that they can be shipped to a rail siding, or so that the lumber industry and the primary industries of Nova Scotia can get into the woods eight or ten months of the year instead of four or five?
Are we talking about subsidies so that we can get from Bathurst to Port Hawkesbury, or from Sydney to Yarmouth without spending two days doing it? Is that what we are talking about? If it is, we welcome that because, yes, that
National Transportation Act
would be a meaningful step ahead. But we do not hear that. We hear from the minister that he is going to assume the authority to do these things if he so chooses. This afternoon the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) said we should be careful about freight rates when buying boats. They have a habit of kicking you in the teeth. That is exactly what will happen in the Atlantic region, if that is not what is intended.
You cannot raise the expectations of the people or play politics with transportation in Atlantic Canada. It is too serious and important. It is too vital to our lifestyle to take away the "at and east" rates from us, but in the mind of the minister I am absolutely certain he considers that to be an inefficient subsidy. What is he going to do with $3 million or $4 million? What roadway is he going to improve? What bus transportation system is he going to improve? How far would that amount go toward providing an adequate feeder aircraft service in the four Atlantic provinces? Not very far.
On the other hand, that is the vital lifeblood of the Port of Halifax and the Port of Saint John, and of grain elevators stretching all the way back to the Lakehead. We are not talking about a dozen jobs. Hon. members will pardon my anger when people play lightly with the jobs of maritimers. They are too damned scarce in the maritimes today. Unemployment there is too chronically high. Hon. members will pardon my justifiable anger. What is the minister talking about? These are some of the questions which have to be answered.
Where is the minister going to get the subsidies? What is he going to cancel? We know about the "at and east" rates. What else is there? We are going to save $200 million on this joint operation, this management passenger sales team? Are we going to get $5 million or $50 million of this $200 million we are losing? Are we going to be so efficient that we will recover enough money to direct elsewhere? What are we talking about, or is that all we are doing, just talking? Do we have some concrete plans? Do we know what we want to do?
I am sorry the minister is not here. I do not know whether he had to be out in British Columbia to make an announcement. Why could that not have been done in Ottawa on the floor of the House of Commons? We have known about this for a long time, but where are these subsidies coming from? What is going to suffer? We cannot help one part of this country by hurting or harming another section of its economy. We want to know the inefficiencies of those subsidies which are not considered to be effective, or which are considered to be less than effective.
I see nothing in here which moves us ahead. If there is nothing concrete, why are we not talking about restructuring the tax system so that there can be an incentive to encourage Canadian owners of merchant ships which are registered offshore for tax purposes? Why are we not talking about that so that we can at least encourage industry, encourage new jobs, and encourage more work for our shipyards? Those are the things we want to know about. There is nothing in this bill. We have not yet had the benefit of hearing the minister speak to us. There has been one speaker from the government side. He

March 1, 1977
National Transportation Act
rambled on about going 45 miles an hour between here and Toronto. Well, hell, he has had ten years to complain about that. Why did he not go to the minister and do it privately to get something done?

speechtext: That wouldn't help.

speechtext:
It probably wouldn't. Until we know what the minister intends to do with this enormous power he is taking for himself and with the right he is giving back to CTC under conditions he will determine and deem to be right in terms of time, structure, and content, this movement back and forth of powers is bound to lead to uncertainty and confusion. And when we have that, we have unrest and an impaired ability to utilize fully the structure because the people simply do not understand it.
We can go on with this reallocation of subsidies program. It sounds great, but until we know what is going to be taken away we are in the dark, and there is not very much we can do.
There are just one or two other items I will touch on because I know there are others who want to speak. They are related more to the institution of the minimum, maximum freight rates, than the discontinuation of the so-called long haul freight rate discrimination which has been built into our system. These provisions are somewhat important, not only to the rail companies, which is obvious, but they also have a serious impact on the trucking industry.
I think we all recognize that shippers who are attempting to broaden their market potential in their part of the country, in other parts of the country and abroad, are going to be very directly affected. As we understand it, the formula set out in the bill is not sufficiently clear to permit the people who will be most directly affected the opportunity at this point in time to make any substantive or in depth comment on whether they will in fact work or whether they will have the long-term effect of working backwards. The present act declares as its goal an economic, efficient, and adequate transportation system, and why not? What else should it have as a goal?

of business for the government which must be logical, reasonable, and honest. Members like myself support this bill. Clearly we have done all this in an effort to carry out original election promises. They are an indication of the direction in which the government wants the country to go.
In the two and a half year life of the present parliament, what has happened to those exciting and imaginative election promises? I would say, little has happened in commuter transit, and in other areas as well. Toronto has sometimes been labelled Hogtown. Perhaps it deserved the label in the past, for its tendency to take more than its share of wealth. That name does not apply to Halton, lying half way between two great cities, Toronto and Hamilton. Somehow, in the consideration of transport questions areas like mine tend to be overlooked. Nevertheless, I still feel-and perhaps I am biased-that suburban areas still count for a great deal in this country.

speechtext:
Suburban life is the butt of a good deal of humour. Nevertheless, there are real difficulties connected with suburban living, and most Canadians are forced into that kind of life. Most jobs are in the city, but most of the places where we live are not in the city. Our people live in the

March 1, 1977
National Transportation Act
suburbs. Mr. Speaker, rush hour traffic is terrible to endure and we must do something about it. The other day I myself was caught in rush hour traffic. Actually I was late for a TV interview on commuter transit and my experience brought the point home to me, especially as I had not undergone such an experience for a number of years.
On paper, the program which the government has put forward looks great. It includes provisions for transit, urban and commuter, for STOL systems for our small, outlying cities; for freight which, God knows, are urgently needed; for western grain, and so on. It could be called the Magna Carta of Canadian transportation. So far as I am concerned the bill is of top priority, for transport in Canada is the glue which holds Canada together, is the lifeblood which nourishes it.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REDEFINE OBJECTIVE OF TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: This bill is going to undo the country.

speechtext:
We hope not.
The idea underlying the original transportation concept involves more than the mere spending of money, although of course it also involves the spending of money. The concept is in two parts, for besides providing better transportation for Canadians it will also bring industrial benefits. For example, there would be the opportunity to provide more jobs in Canadian industry. GM buses would be built in London, Ontario, and Hawker-Siddeley rail cars in Thunder Bay. The policy would enable us to get in on the ground floor of a home grown, indigenous industry, analagous to the American automobile industry. We missed our opportunity with that industry.
We need more industry in this country and our new transport policy will give us the opportunity to create more Canadian jobs, real manufacturing jobs, and not makeshift jobs like those you get under the LIP program, Canada Works, and so on.

The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) spoke on these questions. I agree with what he said. Makeshift jobs are fine for the short term, but they are not our ultimate aim. The creation of more industry and more jobs would also give us greater opportunities for export. We would import less and enjoy a better balance of trade. The policy would lead to a greater use of Canadian national resources in Canada. We should use them here instead of shipping them to other countries which manufacture goods for sale back to us at inflated prices.
The policy will mean greater Canadian control of our own economy, the opportunity for boosting this country's secondary industries, including manufacturing, processing and "value added" items. In other words it will put us right in the ball game, right in line to fulfilling our human and economic values.
This policy offers us the opportunity for more Canadian research, development, and design. It is not merely a money saver and job creator; it is an opportunity to offer our young

people more interesting jobs and greater opportunities. Certainly one of the great purposes of this bill, which follows on the election promise, relates to energy conservation and lowering of pollution. We shall conserve energy as we use less the private car and airplane, and rely more on public transportation, particularly trains.
Finally, I suggest that the purpose of this policy goes beyond the provision of transportation. It would provide the general economic stimulus which this country definitely needs.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-ACTION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES IN VIEW OF HALL REPORT
TRANSPORT-ACTION TO IMPROVE PENSIONS OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES IN VIEW OF HALL REPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I posted for tonight's late show my question having to do with the report of railway pensions by Dr. Noel Hall, I assumed that because we were debating Bill C-33 today the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) would be here and prepared to answer my question. Since he is not with us I presume that a parliamentary secretary will answer for him, and I dare to hope that his answer will be even better than the answer we might have got from the minister.
I addressed my first question on this matter to the Minister of Transport on Friday, January 28, as recorded on page 2493. It had to do with the fact that the Hall report on railway pensions had Finally been published, and since it virtually threw the question of the improvement of railway pensions back to the companies and to the government, I asked the Minister of Transport if he could tell us what steps the government was going to take to try to improve railway pensions. The Minister of Transport answered that the government would take a hard look at the Hall report.
I then asked the minister if he would do something about the specific recommendation made by Dr. Hall calling for the pensions of CPR employees to be brought up to the level of those of the CNR. That, of course, did not get an answer that day.
I returned to the subject on Wednesday, February 23, as reported in Hansard at page 3338. On the general question, I got the same reply I had received earlier, namely, that the government was not yet in a position to give me an answer as
March 1, 1977

to what it was going to do about the Hall report. His exact words were these:
We are continuing to look at what is a very complicated matter.
When I asked the Minister of Transport whether he had had any talks with the CPR about the recommendation made in respect of that company's pensions, he said that he wanted to have a position on the whole matter before talking to someone outside the government.
I think it is interesting that Your Honour is the occupant of the chair tonight. With your railway interest, you must have tried to figure out what the Hall report is all about and why we had to wait two years for it to be produced.
In all frankness, I have to say that railway workers and railway pensioners across this country are somewhat disappointed in this report. It contains a great deal of information in terms of facts, figures, and statistics. It is true that Dr. Hall finds railway pensions terribly inadequate, especially in the case of those already retired and who have had little or no indexing of their pensions. Dr. Hall does make the recommendation that the CPR ought to bring the level of its pensions and the level of that company's indexing up to that of the CNR. He proposes a kind of heritage fund to do something about the inadequate funds of all retired railway workers. However, in terms of anything specific, he literally throws the ball back to the companies and the government. Therefore it is appropriate that questions should be asked of the government as to what it is going to do about the whole matter.
As my previous questions of January 28 and February 23 have indicated, I see this under two general headings. One, there is the specific proposal made by Dr. Hall that the CPR should come into line with the CNR. The other aspect is the whole problem of all railway pensions in Canada.
Dr. Hall says there is no question about it, that those already retired are having a rough time because their pensions have not been indexed. He even goes so far as to say in one paragraph of his report that unless private pension plans can do something about keeping pensions up with the cost of living, their days are numbered.
I shall probably have to raise this matter a good many times judging from the length of time it has taken to get any action. My point tonight is to try to get from the parliamentary secretary an indication of what the government is going to do.
Railway workers and retired railway workers are getting a bit cynical. When the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) appointed the Hall commission two and a half years ago, they accepted that in good faith. I think the Minister of Labour also acted in good faith. However, when two and a half years later the workers and pensioners are handed a report that really does not recommend anything significant, they wonder if the whole operation has just been another snow job.
The government can set aside that cynicism. The government can answer the charge that it is a snow job by saying it now intends to do something. It is not good enough for the Minister of Transport, on the two occasions I put the question to him, simply to say it is a complicated matter, and that the
Adjournment Debate
government will have to take a hard look at it. Pensioners have been waiting a long time for an answer that you, Sir, as a railroad worker, would like to see.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member opposite for raising this matter. Unfortunately he will no doubt agree that this is an issue of such significance that it cannot be comprehensively dealt with in three minutes. He knows that the 277-page report of the industrial board of inquiry on Canadian railway companies pension funds, as submitted by Dr. Noel A. Hall from the University of British Columbia, was published on January 20, 1977 by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro).
The report deals at length with Canadian railway pension funds, a complex and difficult matter. Indeed its highly technical nature made it extremely difficult to arrange for its French translation, which accounts for the delay in publication. During his exhaustive enquiry, Dr. Hall reviewed a number of issues connected with railway pensions. Possibly the most urgent that arose in the course of the study was inflation's repercussions on current pension funds. All along his report, Mr. Hall clearly stressed the need to avoid making recommendations when the parties involved are capable of solving issues of problems within the frame work of the established system of free collective bargaining. The improvement of railway pension funds is one of the areas the solution of which is the responsibility of the parties involved, in Dr. Hall's view, through consultations and collective bargaining. Mr. Hall stresses that unions and companies alike have shown they are capable of dealing with most of pension matters.
In the circumstances, it would seem the government should not intervene in areas that would hinder healthy collective bargaining relations. I should refer to the significant improvements made to railway pensions since 1973, when railway pensions became open to collective bargaining for the first time. To help the parties involved solve the highly complex question as to how pensions should be protected against dollar erosion, Dr. Hall assessed a number of methods for ensuring cost of living escalation under railway pension funds.
The choice of a method, however, is left entirely to the parties involved namely labour and management, in order that their pension and other general priorities may be met. In his study Dr. Hall proceeded at length to compare railway pension funds to other systems.
Mr. Speaker, it clearly stands out from that comparison that in many respects railway pension plans can be favourably compared with the best plans in both public and private sectors. However Mr. Hall did make specific recommendations aimed at achieving more uniformity between the provisions of the pensions plans of the two large railway companies. subtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL REFRIGERATED RAILWAY CARS FOR TRANSPORTATION OF POTATOES
AGRICULTURE-PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL REFRIGERATED RAILWAY CARS FOR TRANSPORTATION OF POTATOES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) is not here this evening I presume his parliamentary secretary will be answering this question, I am delighted to see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lumley) here, as well as some officials from the Department of Transport still in the gallery, because the matter I have to raise clearly pertains to all three departments. It is not new, but it is of fundamental concern to those who come from the two provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.
Perhaps we are fortunate, too, inasmuch as the parliamentary secretary has his roots deep in the province of New Brunswick and I am sure he is very much concerned about the subject I propose to raise, as is his colleague, the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin), who has also raised this matter in the House from time to time. I am sure he shares the view that something decisive should be done with respect to the railway situation affecting the movement of potatoes from eastern Canada.
While I was reviewing the background to this situation today with citizens of Prince Edward Island, we were shocked to discover that the movement of potatoes by rail from Prince Edward Island has been handled for many years entirely by foreign carriers and that the railroads of this country have never supplied any of the cars which have moved potatoes from the island to the central Canadian markets.
I suppose it is another very clear indication of the kind of long-term discrimination which has existed for eastern Canada that we have had to depend so heavily and totally upon the American railroads to supply us with rolling stock necessary to move our potatoes to market. Perhaps we would have gone along in this dependent state into the indefinite future had it not been for the fact that the Americans decided that it was no longer in their interests to carry on with this particular situation. Over the past few years we have seen a very rapid deterioration both in the quality and number of railroad cars available to move our potatoes to central markets.
I was very much encouraged by the comments of the Minister of Agriculture last fall when he made a commitment on one or two occasions to the effect that he was going to make a recommendation to cabinet with respect to ordering somewhere around 800 to 1,000 of these insulated boxcars. However, what disturbed me, not back on January 26 when the motion was put down for an adjournment debate, was the response of the minister yesterday. In response to my question

on whether or not the memorandum was still going forward he said, as reported at page 3464 of Hansard:
-if they would give an absolute assurance-
He is talking about the P.E.I. potato marketing board and the New Brunswick potato growers.
-that they will use these cars and guarantee a certain usage of them-
He went on to include not only the potato growers in the maritimes but the horticultural producers in western Canada, and said he would do something with respect to pursuing the need for more cars. I found this an incredible response, because surely the Minister of Agriculture must know that the absolute decline in the number of rolling stock is exceedingly serious. We have somewhere in the neighbourhood now of 1,000 cars, yet it was only four or five years ago that we were servicing the same situation with 2,500 cars. In fact ten years ago we had well over 4,000 cars.
What the minister was saying was that this year almost all the early orders were going to the export market. So unusually for us, because of the great demand in the European market, many railroad cars sat idle for two months longer than normal before they got rolling some time in December. There was also a change apparently in the United States with respect to the previous per mile charge. They are now renting these cars on a per diem basis, so Canadian National was upset about paying for unused stock.
That the minister would use such an excuse bothered me, because it appears that he may now be prepared to wriggle out or slip away from his earlier commitment, something that I would find both intolerable and unacceptable, and is certainly not in any way dealing with the realities of the situation. In view of the present experience respecting the sale of maritime potatoes to European markets, the minister must know very little about the long-term situation with respect to potato marketing in eastern Canada. Or if he can predict when Europe will be hit with the next drought, I am sure the P.E.I. potato marketing board would be delighted to have him on their staff as a full time weather adviser because that kind of information would be most valuable to them.
I can accept, as I am sure all members can, that there has to be a definite balance between rail and the growing use of highway trailers. Obviously this has not been worked out. But given the existing situation where more of both are desperately needed, surely the minister could get production going now. 1 say this particularly in view of what has happened with respect to the order for grain cars placed at three plants across Canada, but particularly the one placed at the Trenton Car Works. This was referred to earlier in the House by my colleague from Madawaska. Hawker-Siddeley has called back 630 employees to work on the 688 railroad cars which have been ordered for carrying grain. But this is less than half of their total number of employees and, as they have indicated, they could still very actively use an order of this kind to guarantee further employment for about 400 workers who are still out of work, and for whom a job and a return to employment would offer tremendous incentive, and would deal
March 1, 1977

directly with the very high unemployment situation which exists in the Atlantic provinces.
I hope that the minister's parliamentary secretary tonight can assure us that there is no holding up or fooling around with this situation, because I would remind him that last year the minister asked the eastern potato producers to put their own house in order, especially to have more organized marketing, before he could help them in a substantial way. It would be a poor show on his side of the bargain if, after the spectacular success of the potato producers in the export market in Europe, he would not move immediately to deal with our long-term domestic situation and give us an assurance that we would have these domestic rail Cars ordered and in place, or else, quite frankly, we will see the real collapse of the transportation system as it affects both P.E.I. and New Brunswick in terms of servicing the market in the next two or three years.
I know the parliamentary secretary will want to take this question seriously and give that kind of strong assurance to the eastern potato producers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-PROVISION OF ADDITIONAL REFRIGERATED RAILWAY CARS FOR TRANSPORTATION OF POTATOES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to respond to the hon. member for Egmont (Mr. MacDonald) on a question which has been of prime concern, not only to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) but, as the hon. member has said, to several other members of the House for some years, especially members from the Maritime provinces, including the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin) who has on different occasions, I believe, spoken to the minister on this problem. I have noted the keen interest in this subject which has been indicated by members on both sides of the House.
When it became apparent that there were deficiencies in the transportation system for Maritime potatoes, an interdepartmental committee was established by the government to consider all aspects of this very important question. This committee has made significant progress and has kept ministers advised on their findings as they were developed. However, before committing the government to significant expenditures for the purchase of a fleet of new refrigerated railway cars, we must be certain that this would be the best means of assuring the industry of the most efficient means of transportation in future years. Therefore, the consideration that has been given to this question has involved not only whether additional railway cars may be required but also whether the expenditure of government funds in this area would be of the greatest benefit to Maritime potato producers in the years ahead. I am sure hon. members are aware of the advances offered in transportation by such modes as truck transport and containerization.
It has become clear that not only may there be deficiencies in the equipment presently available for the transportation of potatoes, but a very major problem has been the inefficient use of railway cars which are already available. For instance, it has been estimated that a more orderly system of scheduling cars would serve to reduce greatly the problems which now exist during the peak periods of the shipping season. Also of
Adjournment Debate
concern are the storage and loading facilities at the port of Saint John.
It must also be realized that 1976 was a year of good crops and has been most unusual in the export opportunities which have become available to Canadian producers because of the drought experienced last year in Europe. It is unlikely that this volume of exports can be maintained in spite of the efforts of the Potato Exporters' Association in this respect. Therefore it is necessary to assure that railway cars are not purchased solely on the basis of peak demand.
In summary, I would like to assure all hon. members that the government is giving considerable attention to this very important issue and is quite aware of the time constraints which exist.

Mr. Speaker, needless to say
we are gratified to hear not only from his comments tonight but from news stories in his riding that the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) thinks the concept of MAGI is good and that he does not want to lose this type of venture equity.
I am sure that when the standing commitee meets, the hon. member will have an opportunity to question the minister on some of the points he raised tonight particularly as a result of the minister's meeting with the premier of Nova Scotia. Unfortunately I am not aware of the specific details of the minister's meeting with the premier, but it was reported after that meeting that the premier thought the proposed expansion of MAGI to other areas of the province deserved consideration. Based on the hon. member's comments tonight, 1 am sure that he and his party will endorse such a concept.
As the hon. member indicated, I am advised that Mr. Scott MacNutt has accepted the post of chairman of the Nova Scotia Workmen's Compensation Board and has resigned from the vice-presidency and board of directors of MAGI. As the hon. member was informed in answer to a question he raised two or three weeks ago, it is important to put the role of this government with respect to MAGI into proper perspective. It has a management, a board of directors, and shareholders like any other Corporation. It is intended to function much as an ordinary private corporation, and make profits.
The essential difference with MAGI is that its two shareholders are governments. They are not ordinary shareholders. In this regard the MAGI agreement of September, 1972, is quite specific. The agreement states: "The parties are not to intervene in the day-to-day management of the corporation." The shareholders have been careful in ensuring that this has been observed. The day-to-day decisions are and will continue to be made by the board of directors and by management acting for the board. The shareholders do, however, have a unique responsibility for ensuring that the corporation operates within its mandate, that it is well run, and that it conducts itself in a manner which is proper for a corporation whose shareholders are governments.
It is not the role of the shareholders to examine in detail the individual investment decisions of the corporation and to be involved in day-to-day operations. It is their responsibility to ensure good general management, that MAGI carries out its general mandate, and that the investment policies of MAGI are sound. The House may be sure that the minister will be careful to fulfil this role in his communications with the other shareholders and with the board.
